subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE AT ROME-SUGGESTED DEBATE ON CANADIAN POSITION-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a motion to put under Standing Order 43. Yesterday the Canadian Council for International Cooperation concluded a special conference in Ottawa on the world food crisis. This conference brought together representatives of 60 major non-governmental organizations to prepare recommendations for the Canadian government position at the United Nations World Food Conference at Rome starting November 5.
Because of the critical role that Canada, a bread basket of the world, will play at the Rome conference, and because of the great need for non-partisan involvement by parliament, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave):
That a special one day debate be held in the Commons prior to November 5 to examine the recommendations of the council for a strong Canadian position on a world food security system; ways to increase food production in the developing countries; and more equitable distribution of world food supplies.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SARNIA-MONTREAL PIPELINE-REQUEST OF COMPANY FOR GUARANTEES ON THROUGHPUT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In view of indications that officials of the Interprovincial Pipeline Company have been holding discussions with his officials during the past month concerning security of throughput for the proposed line from Sarnia to Montreal, I should like to ask the minister whether his officials have not kept him informed regarding these discussions which go to the heart of the project which the government has considered as being of great importance. I ask this question particularly in view of the fact that the minister made no refer-

October 10, 1974
Oral Questions
ence to any such difficulty in an answer he made in the House on Monday.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SARNIA-MONTREAL PIPELINE-REQUEST OF COMPANY FOR GUARANTEES ON THROUGHPUT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did indeed meet with officials of the interprovincial pipeline company to discuss this as well as other matters relating to the pipeline extension. They indicated at that time their concern on the basis of, perhaps one could say, general comment in the industry rather than on the basis of the National Energy Board report about the availability of oil supplies in the late 1970's and early 1980's. They indicated that their concern principally was related to the financing because of the consequence of any deficiency in the throughput financing. I suggested to them it would be possible to cover such a contingency in the rate structure that would apply. They in turn talked in terms of the possibility of the government securing their position against such a contingency and I suggested to them they should come back with specific proposals if they had them in that regard.
I should say as a matter of interest that I have been advised by the National Energy Board that it has now completed the taking of the evidence in the Montreal pipeline application case, particularly with regard to the changed route, and has adjourned it sine die so that the company can come back to state its position in this regard, as the board said, as expeditiously as possible.

subtopic: SARNIA-MONTREAL PIPELINE-REQUEST OF COMPANY FOR GUARANTEES ON THROUGHPUT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Some of us might wonder why the minister did not see fit to give some indication of some such difficulty when he gave a very reassuring answer in the House on Monday that the matter in his judgment would proceed and be finished early in 1976. May I ask the minister whether the government is prepared to give the pipeline a guarantee of throughput or minimal financial assurance each year or is the government prepared simply to leave this matter stand until the National Energy Board makes its report later on this year as the company has indicated it would either wait for such an assurance or wait until the National Energy Board makes its report.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SARNIA-MONTREAL PIPELINE-REQUEST OF COMPANY FOR GUARANTEES ON THROUGHPUT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
As I think was indicated in the press reports which inspired the hon. gentleman's question, we will be meeting with the company in the course of the coming week to have more precision with regard to its concern about through-put. As I indicated, our feeling is that any financial exposure in this regard should be achieved within the rate structure, but we will want to define more clearly with the company the extent to which it feels financially exposed. Then, of course, at that point the government would have to take a decision concerning what its financial involvement might have to be.
The general principle remains, however. We feel that for the security of the Montreal market the extension should be carried from Sarnia to Montreal.

subtopic: SARNIA-MONTREAL PIPELINE-REQUEST OF COMPANY FOR GUARANTEES ON THROUGHPUT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: The minister refers to me being inspired by a press report. It is fortunate that there is still a free press in this country and that we do not have to depend for information on that minister or any of them.

subtopic: SARNIA-MONTREAL PIPELINE-REQUEST OF COMPANY FOR GUARANTEES ON THROUGHPUT-GOVERNMENT POSITION

subtopic: OIL-ALLEGED POSSIBLE SHORTAGE-SUGGESTED CURTAILMENT OF EXPORTS
OIL-ALLEGED POSSIBLE SHORTAGE-SUGGESTED CURTAILMENT OF EXPORTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a supplementary question to the minister. In view of the fact that the Interprovincial Pipeline Company has asked for this postponement on the grounds that their application was based on misinformation and the oil industry has now reached a conclusion which I have advanced to the minister for the last six months, namely, that by 1980 or sooner Canada will be in a deficit position with reference to oil, and in the light of the reluctance of the Interprovincial Pipeline Company to proceed, is the government considering phasing out our exports of western crude oil to the United States in order to make sure that we have sufficient through-put for eastern Canada, particularly in light of the fact that President Ford has announced that the United States intends to curtail its imports of oil?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-ALLEGED POSSIBLE SHORTAGE-SUGGESTED CURTAILMENT OF EXPORTS
speechtext: It was because of our concern about conflicting opinions on the supply situation that earlier in the year the government asked for an advisory opinion from the National Energy Board with regard to the petroleum supply in Canada. My anticipation is that the government will be receiving a report within a month, and I hope then to have a more definitive indication of the actual supply availability. I have said in general terms, both inside and outside the House, that we anticipate that over the next decade there will be a reduction in Canadian exports of crude oil to the United States. The National Energy Board report when received will provide us with a basis upon which the exports can then be phased down. In sum then, we expect that exports will be going down. The exact timetable, of course, would be better dictated after we have the board's recommendations.

OIL-POSSIBLE SAVING BY USING WESTERN OIL TO SUPPLY MONTREAL MARKET RATHER THAN IMPORTED OIL
speechtext:
May I ask the minister if officials in his department have made any estimates as to what saving would be involved if we could ensure a market in the Montreal area for western crude rather than having to make compensation payments to the oil companies for oil imported. Would such a saving warrant the government in giving an assurance to the Interprovincial Pipeline of a guaranteed through-put?
October 10, 1974

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-POSSIBLE SAVING BY USING WESTERN OIL TO SUPPLY MONTREAL MARKET RATHER THAN IMPORTED OIL
speechtext: My recollection is that 250,000 barrels a day going into Montreal, while reducing the compensation liability, would also reduce the export charge income in the west, and I think that rather than an actual saving there might be a slight net deficit as a result of that kind of change in our supply.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED UNITED STATES ACTION AGAINST AGRICULTURAL TRADE QUOTAS-DISCUSSIONS WITH CANADIAN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It arises out of the statement made public last night that the United States will move against agricultural trade quotas in Canada or put on import controls. In view of the potential seriousness of such a situation, and in the light of the fact that Canadian officials have known of these developments for approximately one month, I should like to ask the minister what discussions Canada has had, other than the discussion which the Minister of Agriculture was supposed to have had when he was in Boise, Idaho?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED UNITED STATES ACTION AGAINST AGRICULTURAL TRADE QUOTAS-DISCUSSIONS WITH CANADIAN GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, following the Canadian government announcement of the quota system, it was indicated to the trading partners affected that Canada was ready to consult with them. Very intensive consultations have already been held with the Americans on the necessity of our establishing these quotas to protect the Canadian market. Subsequent to those discussions at the official level, I raised the matter with Mr. Kissinger when I met him in New York and advised of the serious view that would be taken by the Canadian government of any retaliatory action to the quotas justifiably established by us.

subtopic: PROPOSED UNITED STATES ACTION AGAINST AGRICULTURAL TRADE QUOTAS-POSSIBLE GOVERNMENT ACTION
PROPOSED UNITED STATES ACTION AGAINST AGRICULTURAL TRADE QUOTAS-POSSIBLE GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, as I do not believe the minister really gave me an answer. If a small trade war should develop between Canada and the United States on agricultural products, what will the Canadian government do to alleviate its effects, especially in view of the contradictory statements made in Canada and the United States by the Minister of Agriculture?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED UNITED STATES ACTION AGAINST AGRICULTURAL TRADE QUOTAS-POSSIBLE GOVERNMENT ACTION

At the moment the Americans have filed notice that they propose to take retaliatory action, and we have asked for public presenta-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the reasons I came to Ottawa relates to one of my main areas of concern, namely a concern in respect of water policies, including policies of study and research for the development of a firm resource policy. At this stage I would refer to the only policy we have as a policy of drift. This general state of affairs sems to be further complicated by conflicting comments on the part of a number of Government ministers. There should be active consideration in respect of this whole area of water resources and the export of Canadian water. The concern I express relates to statements expressed once again by ministers in establishing the Liberal position on this subject.
It is my concern that the government is currently negotiating and considering the export of Canadian water. I am led to this conclusion by the statements of various ministers. The former Minister of the Environment, the Hon. Jack Davis, prepared a policy statement for this House which he did not deliver. I am wondering why he did not do so and who stopped him. I have a copy of that proposed statement in which the minister opposed the export of Canadian water. In wondering why it was not delivered I have asked myself if it was because the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) once said in a television interview:
I don't want to be a dog in the manger about this-but if people aren't going to use it, can't we sell it for good hard cash?
Perhaps it was never delivered because of what the Hon. Jean Chretien said, as reported in Time magazine:
-within 25 years we'll be exporting water to the United States-
Was it not delivered because of what Hon. Jack Davis said before the last election when he was trying to jump back on the fence in time for survival, in repudiation of his earlier statements:
I want you to think of water schemes that are not only basin wide but possibly even continental in scope-the Rocky Mountains need no longer contain our thoughts-we can vault over them or tunnel through them and see what lies beyond; so we will be turning whole rivers around.
Was it because of the ghost of the Hon. Arthur Laing who, having just completed an interview, said:
-diversion of Canadian water to the United States is not negotiable- there is no such thing as a continental resource-we own it-
Then, turning aside as he finished his interview, in a supposedly confidential manner he said:
-you should know for your own information that something like North American Water Power Alliance; major water diversion, is not only feasible-it's inevitable. We are establishing a bargaining position and the best position is to say no.
That position is unacceptable to Canadians. As we look at these statements the position of the Liberal government becomes more clear.

October 10, 1974
The Address-Mr. Wenman
Is the new Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Sauve) going to stand up in this House and say the position of the government of Canada is that there will be no export of water? Perhaps the minister would just nod her head at this point. I should like to hear that statement in the next few days, because the pressure is increasing. Demands in the United States for energy will require as much of Canada's water as they can get, particularly when they are following a policy of extraction from shale coal, and the excavation of that coal.
With this kind of pressure we will certainly need all the energy of the minister of energy in preparation for these negotiations, and the non-policy resource statements we have had are completely inadequate.
Only last night in an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen we find the following statement:
Prodded by angry voters back home a month before United States congressional elections, a group of Great Lakes congressmen came out Tuesday for a plan to siphon water out of Lake Michigan-with Canada's agreement if possible, but over Canadian objections if necessary.
Is that to be the position of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) and our Prime Minister? Canadians need to know now. As we anticipate the possible destruction of our precious environment and the establishment of an irreversible trend toward economic and political union with the United States, I am disappointed about what happened in respect of the Prime Minister's previous poetic or perhaps hypocritical statement in which he said:
... If part of our heritage is wilderness and if the measure of Canada is the quality of life that is available to Canadians, then we must act should there be a threat to either-we must act to protect the freshness of our air and we must act to protect the purity of our water; to conserve our living resources. If necessary, we must offer leadership to the world in these respects and withstand the cries of complaining interests.
I ask, where is the leadership today? Where are these statements today? What has happened to the Prime Minister who perhaps spoke for myself and other Canadians when he spoke in this manner? I do not want to be a dog in the manger, but I might ask how hollow these words ring now as the Liberal government is preparing to go forward with the export of water.
Before the Secretary of States for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), or is it Mr. Head, tilts at more new windmills, we need to develop a firm policy against water export. We need strong statements from the Prime Minister and from his chief ministers responsible for energy, resources and environment. Can any true friend and neighbour of another nation expect Canadians to "Judas" their heritage?
Certainly, I do not blame our great cultural friend and economic neighbour to the south for trying to gain and covet our greatest and most precious natural resource. If I were a citizen of the United States, or a politician there, I would probably also be calling for plans and conferences for the velvet glove seduction of Canada. I too, would be saying what Senator Frank Moss said:
-in the United States, increasingly, the control of water becomes the key to prosperity, growth and economic power in the United States- 
Or perhaps I would even be putting forth veiled threats such as:
-we want to continue to live together on this continent in constructive peace for a long time.
Or, as President of the United States, I too would be instructing the State Department to work out a continental energy deal with Canada. When the United States Ambassador to Canada, Mr. Porter makes threats to Canada regarding oil and other non-renewable resources, I do not blame him for making those threats but at the same time I would say that I have great respect for the intelligence of American politicians and am certain that they would not be foolish enough to cut off their nose to spite their face in retaliation. That would, in the short term, damage Canada severely but in the long term the great loser would be the United States.
United States officials are only too aware that the only real hope of maintaining a high standard of living with consumption and production at anywhere near current levels is to maintain solid relationships with Canada and to establish negotiated resource supply treaties. But if the retaliation is a prelude to serious, tough resource negotiations to be carried on in an attempt to gain Canada's resources for a pittance, then I want assurance that these negotiations will not end up with Canada losing its life blood in the form of export of its water.
Major diversion and export of water from Canada is totally unacceptable now and will continue to be so in the future. When the minister stands up and makes such a statement, as I am sure he will after any amount of research, I want him to add to that statement, not negotiable now or in the future. He should state that this is not a bargaining condition. He should make clear that this is the intent of the government of Canada.
Just briefly, in relation to the appointment of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to a high position on the International Monetary Fund, I must say that on occasion I wonder whether Canada had been placed in the role of a puppet in international financial circles rather than as a nation assuming its rightful place as one of the world's most respected exporting nations. I hope the latter proves to be the case and that the minister will not indeed be the puppet of the big five but rather will be successful in elevating Canada's national stature as a fair but strong arbiter and counsel.
Mr. Speaker, I could not make my first speech in this House without bringing forward the matter of western alienation because it is a topic of real concern to the people of western Canada. It is a matter of concern for all Canadians. The eastern oriented government must make a renewed effort to understand, investigate and resolve the underlying causes of this alienation. Even after the poor showing of the Liberal Party in the west, the message apparently has not gotten through. The problem lies much deeper than just the inequitable freight rates, western subsidization of eastern Canada through equalization grants or the excessive expenditure of government revenue in eastern Canada. It lies much deeper. It lies in the matter of the heart and the eye. The frontbenchers of the government of Canada will have to learn to see with the eyes of a westerner.
October 10, 1974

We have this great French-Canadian culture which is talked about as having heart. I think we do have this feeling and give credit to the French Canadians for making a contribution to Canada in this regard. I hope that that feeling of heart which the ministers have for Quebec will be expanded to western Canada so that, as the Prime Minister speaks in terms of what he thinks about the linguistic demands of Quebec and their relationship to the unity of Canada, he will also think in the same way about the feelings of the people of western Canada. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) will have to remember that he should think of the traffic jams in Vancouver as well as those in Montreal about which he so effectively spoke the other day.
While it is true that Canadian cabinet ministers visiting British Columbia perhaps do not receive the warmest welcome, this may be an indication that they should go there more often to find out what is happening. It would be interesting to study the itineraries of all members of the cabinet over the past couple of years, and then perhaps we would realize the reason many cabinet ministers seem oblivious to the problems of western Canada. Member after member has spoken to empty cabinet benches in this House. It is unfortunate that these ministers cannot even find the time to sit in the House to hear the western members on their own side of the House, let alone members of the opposition. It is unfortunate that as transportation improves in Canada the prairies seem to stretch further and further away, and the Rocky Mountains seem to grow higher and higher so far as this government is concerned.
Speaking in those terms, and having been critical slightly of one or two ministers, I should like to say that the western culture is of extreme importance. That culture should be explained here and should be known here. This is significant as well. As a consequence, I have brought with me samples of this culture. I would ask the attendant to distribute these samples to the Speaker and to the leaders of the various parties. I hope members will enjoy these samples and perhaps comment on them to me later.
It is my hope that as the government considers the forthcoming budget, not only will it consider western Canada specifically but also pensioners generally across Canada. I hope the budget will include measures to reduce the pensionable age from 65 to 60, and that there will be a substantial increase in pensions, which will be not just a cost of living increase but an increase in the basic allowance. As this new parliament presses onward, I hope that measures will be brought forward to eradicate the excesses and abuses of unemployment insurance and welfare, and that consideration will be given to the effects of excessive and rapid immigration into Canada.
Any announcements that have been made regarding the alleviation of the housing problem in Canada, let alone in the greater Vancouver area, have been woefully inadequate. I can only assume that major announcements are being saved for the Budget speech. I look forward to these announcements and to commenting upon them at that time.
The Address-Mr. Wenman
I should like to conclude with a short comment concerning one of the most serious problems involving my constituency. Simply put, we are threatened every year by the possibility of devastating floods. The time to talk about the flood protection program is not next May or June, but now. The record of past governments is anything but encouraging. It look 20 years, from 1948, to agree upon a 10 year program of diking and drainage of the lower mainland. In addition to the millions spent on studies and commission reports, the federal and provincial governments have committed some $60 million-certainly a goodly sum which one would think could produce some results.
Let us look at the results. I am sure hon. members on this side know what I am going to say. It took four years, from 1968 to 1972, to complete one of the 44 flood projects. With this track record, can we expect it will take another 172 years to complete the other 43? Is the government on the other side of the House saying to the people of the Fraser valley: "You may sleep safely in your beds in the year 2074? Is that the kind of promise or the kind of action that we are getting? That is what we are thinking and feeling in my area. This kind of progress is hardly acceptable when a flood of 1948 proportions, which experts agree could occur in any year-not four or five years hence but possibly next year, almost this year-would wipe out a good deal of the province's and nation's prime crop land, cause endless economic and social dislocation for the people who reside in the valley, and cost an estimated five times what the 1948 flood cost, that is approximately $100 million. If you allow that flood to occur, you spend $100 million, and on top of that you still have to spend $60 million on the project that will be required to protect the valley.
Let us look at the record. We had nature's fury in 1948. There were pictures of the flood and great concern over the damage and devastation to the Fraser valley. There was a signal to action by the press and the public expressed in such words as "let us get going; let us not have it happen again". We had a report with the program in 1948. Then, we had an interim report in 1949, and then we had that funny report called "The final report". What do you think is the year of the final report? Do you think it is 1972, 1973 or 1974? No, it is 1950. In 1950, we had the final report on what to do on the Fraser River. I have just started with the first three. We can look at reports year after year. The first one was in 1948; then one in 1951, another in 1952, another one in 1956, another one in 1957, 1958, and so on. Year after year promises have been made but nothing has happened. People of the Fraser valley in British Columbia are tired of waiting. We have shown tolerance in waiting for assistance with the ferries, as the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin) suggested earlier. We can build them on our own, but the safety of the people of Fraser valley cannot wait. We must have action in that regard forthwith, and I look forward to hearing the report of the minister on that.
My constituency stretches from the United States border 80 miles to the north border of Garibaldi Park. Fraser Valley West encompasses over 76,000 voters, the majority of whom reside in the southern portion in or around the cities of Port Moodie, Port Coquitlam, Pitt Meadows, Coquitlam, Maple Ridge, Langley, Matsqui and

Surrey. All these came to light in the 1974 election. I am very proud and pleased to be here as a federal member of parliament from the province of British Columbia.
Because the riding bisects the only available corridor to the greater Vancouver area, every transportation access to the nation's third largest city must pass through the constituency. I am, therefore, only too aware of the transportation mess referred to by the minister. A major transportation policy featuring a central corridor and relocation of existing rail beds is of utmost concern to my constituents. In any over-all transportation policy, two local objectives should be satisfied: first, the relocation of the railway tracks from White Rock-Surrey beaches, and second, the relocation of the north-south railway line from the Abbotsford city core. Both objectives, vital to my constituents, can be accomplished through the establishment of a single north-south line through the Sumas area, a line which would tie directly into a major east-west line through the valley, which would serve all major railroads. This objective is not only feasible, but it is certainly sensible from the standpoint of cost, efficiency, and a highly desirable over-all transportation policy for the lower mainland of British Columbia.
In conclusion, I should like to read a letter that I have received from a 16 year old high school student, president of a British Columbia high school, who wrote as follows regarding his impressions of the session so far:
We are following the political scene as best we can. I heard the Throne Speech the other day and I was angered. I wish someone would tell the Liberals that they should give first priority to the problem of providing the basic necessities of life (adequate housing, food and gasoline) at a reasonable cost, and settling once and for all a positive way of solving labour-management wage settlements without strikes which paralyze the economy.
Those are pretty intelligent thoughts. In conclusion, I want to say that it is not 60, 50 or 40 year olds, it is all Canadians who have this concern which I share, and it is on their behalf that I speak.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That shows the great confidence they have in me, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to underline some of the major principles and accomplishments of the energy policies that my department and this government have developed and followed. I should like to refer to all five major sources of energy: oil, natural gas, hydro, coal and uranium-especially uranium as applied for nuclear purposes. Especially, however, I want to speak of oil which because of its availability, its mobility and its versatility is the major energy commodity. It is the standard not only in Canada
October 10, 1974

but throughout the world by which all other energy commodities are managed. Hence, a start on energy policy must commence with oil, and particularly the measures taken in the past 12 months to deal with an unprecedented change in the world oil economy.
Two events in the past 12 months have brought about change in oil policies and, in a very substantial degree, in all energy policies during the same period. The two events are the Arab oil embargo of just a year ago attendant upon the so-called Yom Kippur war, and the two-step increase by which the exporting country tax on oil increased by 410 per cent. As a result, for all importers of oil-North America, Western Europe and indeed throughout the world-the price of oil imported went up by the same percentage.
Canada was in a far better position than most of her OECD partners to sustain the shock during this period. Due to effective co-operative action by the government of Canada and industry, while citizens of other nations in the world suffered fuel shortages this past winter and spring, while our neighbours across the border had to endure frustrating lineups to get gasoline, we in Canada suffered no such problems.
This parliament created the Energy Supplies Allocation Board with the specific responsibility to develop contingency plans against the repetition of that event. At the same time, Canada participated in the development by the Energy Co-ordinating Group at Brussels, of the International Energy Plan. Under this proposal, at the international level the consuming nations may cushion themselves and each other against any future production cutback.
The price of oil for Canadian users was frozen through last winter and then following the meeting of first ministers in March, was restrained at a single price level across Canada-subject to transportation differences-giving Canadians the lowest average crude oil price of any nation in the western industrialized world. The national accord on price which has been accepted by all regions, producing and consuming, was enshrined in the Petroleum Administration Act, Bill C-18 of the last parliament, which will be reintroduced in this parliament.
Let me underscore the tenets of our petroleum policy. First, we have decided that the price of Canadian oil should be set at a level high enough to bring on additional supplies for Canadians without going to the high levels now set by the OPEC group. Second, we decided that there should be a single price of oil for all Canadians subject only to differences for transportation costs. And, third, we decided that in supply we should direct policy toward self-reliance by Canadians on our own oil supplies and that the Canadian pipeline network should be extended accordingly. The price until the end of June will be held at $6.70 per barrel at Edmonton. There is in prospect in the coming months further federal-provincial consultations of the kind that took place last winter to determine where the single oil price for Canadians should go.
In international sales, the National Energy Board determines every month that Canadian crude is being sold for a fair and reasonable return abroad. The difference between that export price and the domestic price is then collected as an export charge. The revenues from this charge are and have been used as a cushion for consumers in eastern
The Address-Hon. D. S. Macdonald Canada, primarily the Atlantic provinces and Quebec, for the purpose of attaining the one price policy for all Canadians.
Let me underline an essential point in this regard. Even if the revenues from this charge were not directed toward this cushion, Canadian crude would still be selling at the same international price in the export market. That is a point I have been stressing to our American customers. I should like to repeat the words that are used in a speech in Washington last week. I said:
The price to U.S. consumers did not go up because of the export tax; rather the Canadian price followed international prices-the prices that we have to pay for oil in eastern Canada. The export tax was a purely domestic impost-the means of determining among different Canadian interests, consuming and producing, who would get the benefit of the economic rents. To fulfil our aim of easing the burden of our eastern consumers of higher offshore prices, we used instead these new returns from export sales as a cushion. We believed then, and still do today, that this is purely domestic matter.
Those were my words, Mr. Speaker, and that is my belief. At the same time, I want to make it clear that Canada is as interested as any other consuming nation in seeing the international price of crude oil reduced by one, two or three dollars. As I told my American audience last week:
We in Canada, as consumers of imported oil, are as unhappy as anybody else about the dramatic nature of the price increase and would be as happy as anyone else to see a reduction in the costs of imported oil.
Further than that, Mr. Speaker, we are in full support of any attempt to negotiate a reduction in the international price for oil, and stand prepared to offer any aid we can to bring the oil producing nations and the oil consuming nations to the negotiating table.
There are two other features of our future planning of oil policy that I want to bring to the attention of honourable members. First is the study of crude oil supply and demand that the National Energy Board has completed after holding extensive hearings where all parties had the opportunity to put forth their views. I expect to receive from the board that report along with its recommendations toward the end of this month. The findings will give the government a sound foundation to continue to tailor federal energy policies to the future requirements of Canadians.

The second point I would like to stress and which concerns future plans in the field of oil is the following: our government will not renege on its promise to build a pipeline to Montreal.
I believe there is almost unanimous agreement in our country to improve the security of our supplies, support our policy and ensure that a greater number of Canadians may, in the future, count on safe Canadian sources for their oil needs. That is what I meant today when I said during the oral question period that we intended to continue with this project and negotiate if necessary with the companies to materialize this project which is so important for the security of Canadians.

October 10, 1974
The Address-Hon. D. S. Macdonald
Now I would like for a minute to turn to natural gas where again my department and this government have formed and are following a consistent and, above all, realistic policy.
Our policy is to bring the price of natural gas in line with the market values of competitive fuels, both to conserve a valuable non-renewable resource and to stimulate development. We intend to do so in a staged fashion to cushion the impact on both United States and Canadian consumers. As I have announced, the border price of a thousand cubic feet of gas will be set, with the exception of one contract in British Columbia, at $1 on January 1. The B.C. contract will be effective from November 1.
This announcement did not come as a bolt out of the blue to our American neighbours. More than a year ago in a speech delivered in Arizona on my behalf, we asserted and I quote:
It is important to note, as many of you are aware, that natural gas pricing is currently very inflexible in both Canada and the United States and it will require alteration of current export contracts and a flexible system of price redetermination if Canada is to receive full market value for its exports of natural gas to the United States.
It is not without interest to note that in the president's statement to congress the day before yesterday, he adopted the same approach with regard to the deregulation of natural gas in the United States. The decision to seek from congress authority to deregulate the gas price is so that the price of gas passing in interstate commerce in the United States can be subject to the same competitive developments of the kind we are trying to introduce in Canada. I assume they will follow the same policy we are following. They will stage increases to consumers over a period of years to make certain the impact is cushioned as far as that may be possible and so that the economic effects will not be disruptive.
This might be a good point to remark on one other important aspect of our policy on oil and gas, and that relates to transit. Some months ago this government initiated a proposal for a treaty between Canada and the United States covering the security of oil and natural gas pipelines. Canada has an abiding interest in this regard, since crude oil from the Canadian West moves by pipeline through the U.S. midwest to reach central Canada, while our refineries in the Montreal area are supplied with offshore oil by a pipeline from Portland, Maine. Some of the natural gas from the Canadian west also moves by pipeline through the U.S. to western Ontario.
We of course have never before felt the need for a treaty to cover the security of these pipelines on such friendly foreign territory, but since the United States has shown an interest in ensuring that the security of any pipeline along the Mackenzie River Valley is covered by treaty, the time would appear propitious to reach an official undertaking that would bestow mutual benefit.
Negotiations toward this treaty are advancing steadily and their success will have an added beneficial effect on the relations between our two countries. As you know, Mr. Speaker, there are some voices in the U.S. who for their own corporate self-interests are questioning the security

of a pipeline along the Mackenzie to move Alaskan gas by pipeline and then by tanker to the U.S. west coast.
A treaty will hopefully still these voices that attempt to aggravate the relations between our two countries that have long stood firmly on a tradition of trust. With these unfounded criticisms laid to rest, our two countries should be better able to judge if there are economic benefits for both in moving Alaskan gas to the lower 48 states and Mackenzie Delta gas to Canadian markets through a pipeline along the Mackenzie Valley.
I would like to turn next to coal. It is readily apparent that the domestic demand for coal of some 27 million tons last year will increase greatly in the years ahead. The study published by my department a year ago last June entitled "An Energy Policy for Canada" set the minimum target for Canadian coal production at 37 million tons per year by the end of this decade. Last year we produced 22.5 million tons, but about half of this production was exported from Alberta and British Columbia, principally to Japan. Meanwhile we imported more than 17 million tons from the United States, mainly into Ontario for both thermal and metallurgical purposes.
Moreover, in the current climate of coal supply in the United States, there is little chance of negotiating new long-term contracts because of the fluid price situation. As of April 1, the U.S. suppliers to Ontario Hydro, with long-term contracts amounting to nine million tons per year, have increased the f.o.b. mine price by 50 per cent. This, added to an increase in U.S. railway freight rates, has made western Canadian coal reserves not only important from a self-sufficiency standpoint, but also of interest in an economic context. Ontario Hydro has therefore focused its attention on locating coal reserves in western Canada as similar as possible to the U.S. high volatile bituminous coal currently being consumed in thermal stations.
The federal government has been following closely the development of arrangements through the national railways, particularly directed to a terminal at the Lakehead for the purpose of developing better coal shipments from western Canada. We have been concentrating attention as well on research and development in technical and economic problems of supplying markets in central Canada with western coal. I wonder if this might be an appropriate time to call it one o'clock.

AFTER RECESS

October 10, 1974

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the House recessed for lunch I was setting out a conspectus of the energy scene in Canada, with particular reference to petroleum, natural gas and coal. With respect to coal I had referred to the fact that while the primary development of this resource, and indeed its use, has rested with the provincial governments, the federal government has been active from the standpoint of carrying out research and development on the technical and economic aspects of supplying western Canadian coal to eastern Canada, and in particular in improving the rail shipment and lakehead transfer of coal so that it will be available for users in the eastern part of the country.
Moving from the subject of coal to electric power, one of the principles set out at the first ministers' conference in January and agreed upon at that time, I think by all the participants, was the desirability, particularly in power-short parts of the country such as my own province and some of the Atlantic provinces, of shifting the generation of electricity from fossil fuels to a secure and economical source such as uranium. Federal policy in this regard has been to provide, as has already been done in the case of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, financing for one half of the cost of the first nuclear plant in each province. It was pursuant to this policy that Canada's third nuclear province was inaugurated yesterday with the announcement that the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission would proceed with the construction of a 600-megawatt equivalent nuclear plant at Point Lepreau in the Bay of Fundy. At the same time, as further federal policy we have provided an outstanding offer to carry half the cost of regional electrical interconnection studies, as well as half the cost of financing approved projects which result from those studies.
At the moment there is an extensive examination, with the province of Newfoundland, of the possibility of harnessing Churchill River Power, bringing it across the mainland and under the Strait of Belle Isle, to the island. As well, there has been extensive discussion with the other Atlantic provinces concerning inter connections in that area. One of the benefits to be achieved by the establishment of a nuclear plant in New Brunswick is the provision of a secure supply of power not only for New Brunswick but for the province of Prince Edward Island which, under present federal arrangements, will soon be receiving the benefits of an interconnection under the Northumberland Strait to that island.
On the question of uranium, early last month I announced new guidelines for the sale of uranium by Canada. In the next decade there will be a four-fold to six-fold increase in the annual demand for uranium, both within and outside Canada. Existing and potential production facilities will be strained to meet that demand. In order to provide orderly growth of the industry, while at the same time protecting the needs of our domestic nuclear program, we have concluded that protection of Canadian uranium consumers should be two-fold. First, we should ensure a long-term reserve of nuclear fuel for existing and committed reactors as well as for reactors which are planned for operation in Canada over a future period of ten years. Second, we must ensure that sufficient uranium productive capacity is available for the Canadian domestic nuclear power program to reach its potential.
The Address-Hon. D. S. Macdonald
Not only are we seeking to make certain, by reserve formulas and by our export policy, that there will be uranium available for Canada from existing sources, but through the Crown-owned nuclear corporation, Eldorado Nuclear, we have provided substantial additional budgetary funds to permit that corporation to undertake extensive exploration for uranium. This program is now under way. As part of the program of putting Eldorado Nuclear once again out into the prospecting field, we are pleased to have attracted to the service of this country Mr. Nicholas Ediger whose experience and success is well recognized in the private resource industry. He is undertaking the role of president and chief executive officer of Eldorado Nuclear.
Time does not permit me to review all the prospects for Canadian CANDU reactors. I merely say that with the increase in the cost of fossil fuels, the CANDU system-as evidenced by the outstanding performance of the Ontario Hydro plant at Pickering-has become very much in demand and inquiries are being received from many countries about the possibility of acquiring these reactors. And such sales would, of course, be subject to further safeguards, not only to ensure that nuclear material was not used for military purposes but to provide restrictions against its use for nuclear explosions whether deemed peaceful or not.
I have tried to put forward some of the major elements of our energy policy. In the coming weeks and months additional measures will be placed before the House. While it is true that Canada is well endowed with the five major source of energy, our policies must be tailored to ensure that Canadians continue to have access to these sources at reasonable cost both environmentally and in terms of dollars and cents. Threats to the environment, and the dramatic increase in the monetary cost of energy experienced in recent months, show the need for policies based on a firm federal overview of Canada's resources.
Before closing I would refer to a question raised by a previous speaker on the export of water from Canada. Since 1968, when I first became a member of cabinet, no proposition has been put to the cabinet proposing such export from Canada, and there is no grand scheme, as the hon. member intimated, for the export of this nation's water resources. Indeed, I am glad to repeat that since I have been in this House I have been unable to see any basis at all for Canada's ever agreeing to export so fundamental a product and commodity as water, particularly in the great plains area where water is so essential and valuable to Canada's ambitions in that area, both industrially and agriculturally.
With regard to the Chicago water diversion, the hon. member might want to refer to the record. Indeed, the Chicago water diversion at the start of this century was one of the reasons for establishing the boundaries water treaty. As a resident of the Great Lakes area, he may be assured-as all hon. members may-that as a member of this government I will make every effort to prevent any further diversion of water out of the Great Lakes' system into Lake Michigan, whether for industrial reasons or otherwise.

October 10, 1974
The Address-Hon. D. S. Macdonald
In the months to come we will be considering, as part of the government's program, the petroleum administration act. We will be considering, as well, the establishing of Petro-Canada, the national petroleum corporation. In particular, later in the year we will be dealing with guidelines regarding the ownership of Canadian uranium and Canadian uranium resources. We are looking forward to continued active discussion of those questions in the House and in committee, and I will be glad in private and in public to have exchanges on this important area with members from all sides of the House.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question through you, Mr. Speaker. Inasmuch as the minister talked about the equal price of gas and oil across Canada, and that it would be government policy to differentiate petroleum products from, say, textiles, automobiles and farm machinery, I ask the minister how petroleum products reach that particular status.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Basically, Mr. Speaker, most products in Canada are sold at the same basic price subject only to transportation charge differences. In this respect petroleum is treated no differently from any other product. The different aspect of the policy-one which, as I have said, has been agreed to by all ten premiers and the first minister of this government-is that, given the peculiar nature of petroleum, the essential character of petroleum not only in this but in all other industrial societies, the government views it in the interest of Canadians to ensure that the high price of international oil that has been set by the OPEC countries should not dictate petroleum prices in this country. For this reason we have set as a national policy a single price for petroleum, subject to transportation charge differences, maintaining that price at a level below that of the international commodity.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize hon. members want to participate in this debate, but may I put one question to the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

My question concerns a Mackenzie delta pipeline for natural gas, not for oil. I am taking into consideration the fact that a regulatory body would have control over the pipeline, as the minister has pointed out. Has the government given serious consideration to a pipeline through which to transport natural gas, and has it worked out an equitable and reasonable agreement with the United States, in view of the high cost of building such a pipeline? Has the minister had discussion with the United States with a view to bringing natural gas down the Mackenzie delta in order to supply a product that is

important not only to western and eastern Canada but, indeed, to the United States itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has indeed been discussion of a Mackenzie Valley gas pipeline with the American authorities. As the hon. member knows, under a law of this parliament, parliament has entrusted, in the first instance, the National Energy Board with responsibility for scrutinizing this kind of pipeline application and making a decision thereon. What I say will be subject, of course, to the information that will come from the gas availability studies which the National Energy Board is now carrying out, and will be carrying out at hearings in Calgary and Vancouver, to determine the time-frame in which Canadian users will need so-called Arctic gas. But it is clear that within the same time-frame the availability of natural gas in Canada will depend upon delivery of gas from the frontier, whether the high Arctic, Labrador or the Mackenzie delta. In this sense, the question is not whether there will be a pipeline; ultimately there will have to be one if we are to have natural gas in this country. The only question, is, when. The government's conclusion in this regard is subject to the prior obligation of the National Energy Board to scrutinize proposals.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to ask a question which might clarify a brief reference the minister made?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas).

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The minister made a brief reference to safeguards with respect to nuclear power plants so as to ensure that nuclear power will be used solely for peaceful purposes. In view of the fact that these safeguards have so far proven ineffective, as demonstrated by the actions of India in producing the capacity for making a nuclear bomb, may I ask the minister what additional safeguards the government has in mind to ensure that safeguards will be much more effective than they have been up till now?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must correct the hon. gentleman when he says the safeguards have been ineffective. It is clear from the nuclear explosion in India that they used the benefits of the research reactor supplied to them in the fifties by the United States and Canada at a time when safeguards were not established at the international level and before the present system of safeguards had evolved.
The subsequent Canadian nuclear reactor and technology supplied for power purposes are covered by safeguards, as indeed are further supplies of technology. In this sense one cannot blame the current system of safeguards for the action India may have taken, using a research reactor not covered by the safeguard systepa. The government of Canada over the years sought to include that research reactor under the safeguard system. For reasons now obvious, India refused to co-operate and I think we all regret that she took the action she did.
Since May 18, the date of the explosion in India, the policy of the government regarding the transfer of nuclear
October 10, 1974

technology and, indeed, the sale of uranium itself has been not only to stipulate the international level of safeguards but to stipulate a higher level of safeguards by bilateral agreement in order to ensure that uranium or technology in connection therewith will not be used for nuclear explosions whether described as peaceful or not.
The legal argument raised by the government of India was that the international system permits the development of an explosive for peaceful purposes. Canada does not accept that. Once you have this technology, it cannot be misapplied in other directions, and we have put this further requirement upon nuclear sales by this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does that include the spent fuel, too?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, the safeguards include the spent fuel. I think one of the questions Canada should involve itself in over time is not only safeguard requirements and inspection by the International Atomic Energy Agency but whether we should stipulate in all sales that the spent fuel, plutonium, be returned to this country so that it would not be available for other applications.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps what has just occurred shows that the question period will come to an end of its own volition even if we do not have a time limit. I should like to begin by congratulating the new Speaker upon the elevation to his high position in the House of Commons. I am sure all hon. members wish him success in the execution of the exacting duties that his office entails.
I wish to reflect briefly upon the recent election and devote the major part of my speech to the subject of national defence. Canada seems to have had two elections this summer, one in western Canada and the other in the rest of the country. The only similarity was in their both being on July 8. In the west, the Progressive Conservative Party gained seats-in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia-and they were denied doing so in Alberta only because they already held 100 per cent of the seats there. In my province of British Columbia, the Progressive Conservatives, who held no seats two years ago, now hold a majority of seats. During the recent election, the Conservative received approximately 42 per cent of the vote, the Liberals 33 per cent and the NDP 23 per cent. I have introduced this point to serve as a backdrop for a question that concerns me greatly, that is, the continuing and growing alienation of western Canada from the rest of the country. The conduct of the campaign and the result of the federal election have contributed to this alienation. Despite the fact that westerners are demonstrably on a three-party system, the four western provinces have for the second election in a row voted overwhelmingly Conservative. In the last election, 72 per cent of the western members returned to this House are of that party, yet the west is now faced with a government which does not understand their problems and has been manifestly incapable of solving them.
The election is over and the Liberals won. However, I do not think that those occupying the government benches are entirely pleased with the manner in which the election
The Address-Mr. McKinnon
was conducted by their party. I believe there are men and women of high principle in the Liberal party, and it is this group which must surely feel some disquiet or remorse over the methods employed during the campaign. The different approaches to the election seem to be typified in two quotations, one by the leader of the Conservative Party who at a very difficult time in the campaign said: There are some things in life more important than winning an election.
On the other hand, a well-known Liberal said:
Whatever is necessary to do to win the election, that I will do.
The second quotation typifies that which I found most objectionable about the election. Any party which subscribes to the motto, "Whatever is necessary to do to win the election, that I will do" is subscribing to a philosophy that many Canadians find abhorrent. Indeed, to honour such an expediency by giving it the status of a philosophy is little more than effrontery. This Liberal ethos may explain their lowering themselves to playing upon ethnic prejudices. How else is one to explain Liberal advertising in Quebec urging the Quebecois to vote against "Mr. Stanfield" and to vote for "Monsieur Trudeau"? The leader of the Progressive Conservatives is surely the last Canadian politician who deserves to be the object of such bigotry. Those who plead for votes for the Liberal Party as the party of unity should be deeply shamed by such racist attacks upon our leader during the last election campaign.
Let us consider, now, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), that man of integrity who can look into the colour TV cameras with his china-blue eyes and say, "I believe in levelling and being honest with the Canadian people". Why did this man remain silent when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was making promises that the Minister of Finance knew could not be kept? I can only conclude that his principles are not as lofty as he would wish us to believe and that he, too, would do whatever is necessary to win an election. In remaining mute on the mendacity implicit in the Prime Minister's promises, his expediency was that of silence and omission. Perhaps the minister feels there is moral superiority in committing sins of omission rather than sins of commission. I should like to remind him of the well-known quotation, "If you're not part of the solution, you're part of the problem".
Another nefarious tactic of the Liberal Party was the blatant use of the Senate of Canada as a campaign headquarters. The national campaign chairman was a senator; the campaign chairman in British Columbia was also a senator. These people are appointed to office to serve their regions and all Canadians in their regions, not just to serve the Liberal Party. However, it is quite clear that not only does the Prime Minister expect them to serve the Liberal party during election campaigns but he rewards them for doing so. The Prime Minister speaks of reform of the Senate. The first reform should be to ensure that he does not use senators in the manner in which he used them last summer, when in fact a large part of the Liberal campaign committee was paid for, unwittingly, by the taxpayers. The government had four western ministers before the election. One was defeated, one was demoted and two were returned with reduced majorities. I would like to compliment the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) for narrowly avoiding the fate of the minister

of fisheries or the fate of the former minister of urban affairs.
It has become apparent over the last few years that the only opportunity one has to speak on defence in this House arises during either the throne speech or the budget speech. Despite the fact that defence is crucial to our national and international stature, it has served the purposes of the government to give the Department of National Defence the lowest possible profile among government departments. I would not like to imply that the Minister of National Defence and the government intentionally misled the Canadian people about Canada's defence position before the election, but there is a rather remarkable difference between the statements the minister made a year ago and those he has made recently.
What has changed most is that a year ago the government was in a minority position, faced with an election, and now it is in a majority position and will not have an election for some four years. This change in circumstances may account for the startling reversal of the minister. About a year ago, the minister put out a document explaining the wonderful things he was going to do for Canada's armed forces. Now, in the revealing light of post-election reality, he has changed that position drastically. I would be pleased to see the minister stand in the House and speak on defence. The hollowness of the minister's promises of last October, when he said he would be able to increase the capital budget of the armed forces substantially, to enable it to purchase additional and new equipment by virtue of this 7 per cent increase, I suggest is sheer mockery. Any housewife in Canada realizes that with a 7 per cent increase in your budget over that of 1973 one cannot do anything but cut losses and reduce purchases.
Inflation did not start on July 8; it started several years ago and was running at a much higher rate than 7 per cent at the time the minister made his statement. Now that the election is over, the minister said, after being questioned in the House, "Cuts will have to be considered in all areas-operating, personnel and capital expenditure." Our troops have been operating on a very skimpy budget over the past six years. They have been forced to reduce their numbers, to cut back on their equipment and to defer plans for modernization. Now a program is to be brought in which will make the past six years look like days of roses and wine to the troops. Whenever Liberal governments want to restrict expenditures, they always seem to look at defence. This is hardly surprising, I suppose, for one should remember these words of the Prime Minister:
I would like to have generals looking at our whole military machine and saying, "You know this is not really important today".
Something will have to give; the government cannot continue loading role on top of role upon the armed forces while simultaneously throttling their budgetery purchasing power. Let us consider the armed forces in somewhat greater detail. I shall, perhaps, be excused for referring to the navy, army and air force-terms meaningful to most Canadians. In their unification, the various "elements" share one dominant characteristic: they are all short of equipment. The navy, perhaps, has had slightly higher capital budgets relative to the other two forces. This seems

to have been due to a concept popular in the late 1940s when it was decreed that Canada would specialize in anti-submarine warfare. The military situation in the world has changed a great deal over the last 25 years. I believe that in the current situation this overly narrow specialization in the submarine detection role has been harmful to the general operating capability of the force. The central task required of Canadian marine forces in the near future is not likely to be submarine detection but, rather, the preservation of sovereignty over the waters adjacent to our coasts.
At the same time as Canada is extending claims of sovereignty over these areas and is hence demanding more of the navy, a cut-back in personnel has required our navy to lay up ship after ship. The minister has been, unsuccessfully, trotting around the countries of the world in an attempt to lease out these ships presumably on some sort of a "U-Drive" basis. What a sorry spectacle! However, in comparison with other services the navy is fortunate in that it has something in the way of new equipment: it has four DDH-280 destroyers which are probably among the world's finest anti-submarine vessels. They are doubtless among the world's most expensive. Their cost has never been fully divulged, and I hope that during this session the minister will see fit to answer questions which will appear on the order paper concerning the cost of the DDH-280s. Now that the last of the four has become operational with the fleet, there no longer exists the minister's faint excuse for not divulging the cost to the previous parliament.
No doubt these ships and their men are extremely efficient and well suited to a submarine detection role. But is this the role for which we should be preparing our navy, or shall we find ourselves in the unsatisfactory position of having the equipment determine the role? As I said a few moments ago, the role which I see for our navy in the foreseeable future will not be solely anti-submarine but protection of the sovereignty of our coastal waters. A more unlikely vessel than the 4,500-ton DDH-280 to accomplish this task is hard to conceive, particularly when one considers that the surface-to-surface capability of these $75 million destroyers is almost non-existent. We live in a world where surface-to-surface missiles with an over the horizon capability are being mounted on gunboats, and a match between a gunboat which costs around $6 million and our new destroyers would surely find the smart money being bet on the gunboat.
Let us now consider the air force. Here the capital equipment problem is most acute. The CF-104 located in Germany recently has gone through an expensive conversion to enable it to fire cannon instead of being armed with atomic weapons. Our allies in Europe are looking toward the next generation of fighters. They have developed the MRCA multiple-role combat aircraft. We have not yet been told why Canada was not involved in the research and development of this aircraft. In Canada we have two squadrons of CF-5s. The kindest thing I have heard said of the CF-5 is that every emerging nation should have one. The big and expensive concern in this area is, of course, the longrange patrol aircraft which is to replace the four maritime patrol squadrons of aging Argus aircraft which are with the maritime element. The cost of this replacement is edging close to the billion dollar mark,
October 10,1974

and as our modernization program apparently is to be geared to the availability of money and not the need for the aircraft, I wonder if this government is really likely to replace the Argus in the near future.
The interceptor squadrons of air defence command fly the F-101C aircraft, which probably is the only plane in our forces which is appropriate for the role it has been given. I am not at all convinced this role is right and proper for Canada. However, I will deal with that matter a little later. To sum up the situation in respect of the air element, we are looking at the replacement of two aircraft for an extremely large sum of money, something like $2 billion. For long-range patrol aircraft replacement the government has considered the Orion and a Lougheed redesigned 707. We have spent $11 million this year and have asked the aircraft company to submit further studies. In either case we are considering buying ten-year old foreign aircraft and will be replacing aged aircraft with middle-aged aircraft. We seem always to be hoping to get the last of the production run from an American factory.
Finally, let us consider our ground force, the army. It is a strange experience to visit army camps in Canada. Half of the army personnel appear to be living or training in an uncertain future, while the other half are living or training in the distant past. There are helicopters in use, on the one hand, and 25-year old guns on the other. Although this applies to many other pieces of equipment, I would mention as an example the handling by the Canadian government of the purchase of tanks for our army. One could quote Hansard chapter and verse over the last few years to illustrate that the army was to be given tanks almost immediately. Such statements go back to the days of Edgar Benson.
The government has procrastinated and equivocated on this matter and now Canada's finest armoured troops are equipped with 30 Centurion medium tanks of 1946 vintage. It might be of interest to the House to put this matter in perspective. The International Institute for Strategic Studies, military balance for 1973-74, at page 95 sets out the main battle tanks held in central Europe. NATO formations hold 6,755, Warsaw Pact nations 13,800, and Canada 30.
The minister, before the dissolution of the last parliament, announced that he did not intend to replace the Centurion tank at that time. I understand he will participate in this debate. I ask him to make a statement on the future of the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps so that the men of that force will know whether they will be given a replacement for the tank, whether it be an armoured car or another tank, or whether they are to be transferred willy-nilly into other corps. This is the lifetime occupation of these men, and I believe they have a right to know.
Having considered the equipment of the three components of our forces, it should be abundantly clear that, as General Simonds-one of the truly great military figures of our country-once said cynically, indeed Canada has a military policy: the forces will recruit troops in times of high unemployment and will buy equipment when the government desperately needs to keep an industry alive. The fact that the government has given the forces roles which demand modern equipment should carry with it a commitment that it will provide the necessary equipment.

I should like to say a few words about NORAD. The committee on external affairs and national defence tabled a report a year ago last April recommending that the NORAD agreement not be signed for another five years but for two years only, and that in the ensuing two years an extensive and in-depth examination of the value of our role in NORAD should be undertaken. That resulted in Canada signing a two-year agreement to extend NORAD, I believe on May 12, 1973. This agreement expires on May 12, 1975. Some 18 months have gone by, and not one meeting of the defence committee has been held with that subject on the agenda. Again the time is becoming short before the treaty must be renewed or cancelled. In a very few months from now we will be forced to make another hasty decision on one of our most important international agreements.
I do not wish to make a definitive statement about the value of NORAD because I realize, if the government does not, that there is need for such a study before members make up their minds on this important matter. NORAD is not an ordinary alliance between two countries; it is an intermeshing of the components of our forces which are engaged in the air defence of our continent. We should know what we are doing before we try to upgrade NORAD. Let us study the matter to see whether the role Canada is playing is the one that Canadians want to play. We must think of the cost to Canada of being involved in NORAD.
A cost that we must consider is that in the attempt to counteract 7 per cent of the atomic threat to this country we agreed to accept, and still accept, atomic warheads on Canadian soil. That was some 15 years ago, so it is time we took another look at that program. I do not praise it or condemn it, but I want members of parliament to study the matter and know what they are voting for when the next vote takes place. I hope we will find it a satisfactory arrangement and will be able to offer advice to improve intercountry co-ordination and possibly diminish the enmeshment of our troops so that we will have a little more independence than at present. As an aside on the parliamentary level, let me point out that when the Prime Minister considers reforming parliament he should take into account the fact that the combination of defence and external affairs in one standing committee serves only to hinder the operation of both departments. We should have two committees to deal with matters concerning two departments. Both major parties in the House have for some time two-platooned that committee. I believe this has been to the detriment of both external affairs and national defence. A good example of this is at hand. Last Monday, the external affairs and national defence committee elected its chairman, who was immediately sent to New York. He will be coming back next Monday or Tuesday and we will hold a meeting of the steering committee, at which I expect we will set aside some time to discuss the estimates of the Department of National Defence. However, those estimates must be back in the House by the following Monday, so we shall have only two or three days to consider them in committee. This is a less than 'cursory examination of a $2 billion budget.

They are able to take on roles that would try the patience of saints, and they do this under political direction which seems implacably opposed to treating them as the valuable members of our society that they are. As a member of NATO, Canada should find it embarrassing that in our defence expenditure, expressed as a percentage of the gross national product, we are second to last among the 13 nations listed. If we look at the percentage of people serving in our armed forces, out of men of military age in North America-that is, Canada and the United States-as well as the 19 European nations of NATO and the Warsaw Pact, it shows us to be last on the list.
Worse than that, small as is the budget that we allot to national defence, a more critical statistic demonstrates how the budget is allotted. The International Institute for Strategic Studies points out that in the category "Pay and allowances plus maintenance" Canada spends 89.8 per cent of her military budget. Of the other five nations listed, namely, Britain, France, Germany, Japan and the U.S.A., none spends within 20 per cent of Canada's figure. To understand this one should consider this matter in another way. The percentage of each budget which goes for research and development, equipment and capital costs, shows Canada at 10.2 per cent while the other five nations are listed at over 30 per cent. This is the true test of whether or not a nation is keeping a modern force, properly equipped. It seems to me that in the world situation today one can say there are possibilities for only two types of war-nuclear and non-nuclear. There is no third type. There cannot be a partly nuclear or a limited nuclear war. I do not think the present minister or the government have ever clearly understood that these two types of war are completely dissimilar. Therefore, we find ourselves between two stools: part of our forces are training and planning for a possible nuclear war or a partly nuclear war, and other parts are training to participate in a conventional war. The lack of clear definition from their political masters is the main reason for this uncertainty.
The minister's replies to questions on October 4 and 7 indicate that the budgetary situation of the forces is critical. The minister has been forcing them to subsist on a barebones budget for years, always with the promise that he would use the money saved to buy equipment. There are always two promises which the Liberals make- I am repeating what I said last November 15 as recorded in Hansard-and one is that they will reduce the forces while the other is that they will use the money saved to buy equipment.
