Mr. Speaker, please accept greetings directed at yourself and all honourable members of this House from the constituents of the Northwest Territories. I represent the largest constituency in the world. I believe we are in the Guiness Book of Records. But it is a record of which no one can be very proud. We in the Northwest Territories would gladly give up that honour in the interest of having more representation in this House. In the Northwest Territories there are 1,350,000 square miles, with 40,000 people scattered in some 80 communities, separated not only by large distances, made more difficult by the harsh climate, but also by cultural differences and by language. All this makes the job of representation more difficult than that of any other member of the House. The Northwest Territories comprise a very large land which is very thinly populated. But in fact it has not the smallest population in the country; a number of other ridings have smaller populations. One of these, of course, is the Yukon. Although they have a more compact constituency, at least they have a few more roads than the Northwest Territories.
Of the four ridings in Prince Edward Island, three have smaller populations than the Northwest Territories. In the case of P.E.I. it has been recognized that the principle of strict representation by population cannot always be followed and safeguards have traditionally been applied to ensure that the representation of P.E.I. does not fall below a certain number. This is all to the good; it should be this way. But it should be clear to anyone who has looked carefully at the case that the same principle must apply to the Northwest Territories. It is not possible for one man effectively to represent the whole of the Northwest Territories. To give honourable members some idea of the problems that a member from the Northwest Territories must face, I would mention that the size of my riding is literally the distance from one of our oceans to the other. Simply to visit each community and to spend two days in each would take up eight months of each year. A good deal of this is travelling time alone, and that can change depending on the weather. The weather up there changes very rapidly, especially along the Arctic coast. Some communities cannot even be reached for part of the year, and some can only be reached by charter aircraft. It is impos-
October 10, 1974

sible to get into many communities during the fall freeze-up and the spring break-up.
It is also impossible to get to many of my people through the mails or the newspapers, because many of them cannot read. And in addition to French and English, the people of the Northwest Territories speak at least six separate native dialects. They are separated not only by distance and by climate but by huge cultural differences and equally huge language problems. Travel is made much more difficult, also, by the poorly developed facilities in the north. All our supplies have to be brought in either by boat, in the summer, or by airplane, In most parts of the Northwest Territories the airplane is the only way to get around arid air travel costs much more than in the southern parts of Canada. Here are a few examples, Mr. Speaker. The return fare from Montreal to Toronto is $74, while the return fare from Cambridge Bay to Spence Bay- which is about 40 miles less, in a straight line-is $230. That is a big difference. The return fare from Montreal to Winnipeg is $178, while the return fare from Edmonton to Inuvik, an equal distance, is $312.
There are no government offices for most of my constituents. They cannot walk down the street to a Canada Manpower centre or jump on a bus and go to a government office. It is for these reasons, among others, that I will reintroduce my private member's bill calling for at least two members to represent the Northwest Territories. This will be the third time I have introduced such a bill, and I urge every member of this hon. House to seriously consider it when it comes before them. It is particularly appropriate and important that we look at this issue now, for in the next few weeks we will be considering the question of redistributing seats in the House of Commons. If this issue is not dealt with now, it will be several years before we can look at it again.
While we are on the subject of representation in the Northwest Territories, I would like to mention another important issue. The Northwest Territories do not yet have responsible government. The history books tell us that Joseph Howe, in the first half of the nineteenth century, was called the father of responsible government. I am sorry to say, Mr. Speaker, that in the last half of the twentieth century the Northwest Territories are still not part of that family.
Provincial status for the Northwest Territories has been talked about for years, but it has never been taken seriously. In the next few years this question will become more and more important as the population of the Northwest Territories grows and as vast economic developments take place-developments over which the people of the Northwest Territories have little or no control-and in most cases, no control. It is time to talk about bringing responsible government to the Northwest Territories as the first step to this area being made a province some time in the future. I do not say the Northwest Territories should become a province next week, or even next year. The people of the Northwest Territories must first have some experience in governing themselves. But this will not happen unless we are allowed to elect our own government and unless that government has some control over
The Address-Mr. Firth
funds, over resources and over the economic and social development of the territory.
This lack of control can be seen not only in government but also in administration. There are very few native employees in the territorial government, and very few of these are in positions of responsibility. Out of a total of over 1,600 Northwest Territories employees working in the Northwest Territories in 1972, only 305 were native people. Of the 182 of these classified as scientific and professional, none was native. Neither of the two executives was native. Our governors are imported from the south, and the administrators who carry out their orders for the most part are imported along with them.
Mr. Speaker, the Northwest Territories remains as it was before it was ceded by the Hudson's Bay Company over a hundred years ago, a territory run by and for an absentee governor-a kind of government by remote control. We desperately need programs and services that are taken for granted in other parts of the country, this great land of ours known as Canada. Health services are not just poor; they do not exist for most people in the Northwest Territories for most of the year. The health of my constituents is surely the worst in Canada. In all of the Northwest Territories there are only 16 doctors and 15 dentists. Dental care does not exist in most parts of the Northwest Territories.
I should like now to quote briefly from a newscast on CFFB Frobisher Bay on September 3, 1974, and I would ask hon. members to listen very carefully. Here it is in part;
The lowest nutrition standards and the highest infant mortality rate in North America. That is the grim statistic and according to a Frobisher Bay doctor, the situation is getting worse.
In a random series of tests conducted by Dr. Alex Williams of the Frobisher General Hospital, over 75 per cent of the pregnant Inuit women and young Inuit children examined, showed critically low nutrition levels. In a number of cases, said the former chief of medical staff, vitamin A and vitamin C necessary for the prevention of infection and skin disease, simply were not present. The results, he said, were children, if they survived, who at as little as eight days old, had perforated ear drums, systematic infections, skin sores and almost no resistance to disease. Not only that, the IQ level of children born with these vitamin deficiencies was 20 per cent to 40 per cent lower than average.
Much of this could be improved with training programs for northerners. We can handle many of our own problems if we are given a chance to do it. A government training program that would turn out only ten pilots a year over the next five years would be wonders for this situation. But this would be only a beginning. We need pilots and mechanics, doctors, dentists and nurses. We need airstrips, and we need airplanes to use the airstrips. We need many more navigational aids to facilitate the aviation industry up there. Because of the great distances involved, it is one of the most important industries. Railways in the southern part of this country have been subsidized for generations to the tune of several hundred million dollars. The federal government subsidy for the short takeoff and landing commuter plane between Ottawa and Montreal was over $25 million, by its own figures. In the north, where transportation problems are much more serious, we need the same kind of subsidization. The result of high transportation costs is a cost of living higher than anywhere else in Canada.

For example, Yellowknife food prices are 20.13 per cent higher than those in Edmonton. Here are a few price comparisons for hon. members to think about: chicken in Edmonton is about 87 cents per pound; in Yellowknife, $1.19; medium eggs are 90 cents a dozen in Edmonton, while the Yellowknife price is $1.09. Orange juice is 61 cents in Edmonton; 85 cents in Yellowknife. These prices are low compared with prices along the Arctic coast or the Mackenzie River. In the villages along the river a dozen eggs cost $1.98 or $2, if they are available.
We need funds, not hand-outs, for economic development. We would like funds that we can put to use where we see need, whether it be training programs, setting up small businesses or whatever is necessary. The government of the Northwest Territories develops programs that look good on paper, but when people come to apply for a loan to set up a small business somewhere, or a restaurant or a shipping company, they run into a lot of red tape. All hon. members know what I am talking about when I say we have to cut red tape. Down here you can at least cut it. We have more serious problems. Up there we have to cut the tape lengthwise.

If the unemployment rate goes up in the next few months, as it probably will, it will make little real difference. The people of the north, and native people all over Canada, are in a permanent depression that makes the 1929 crash look tame by comparison. The Metis people of northern Saskatchewan, for instance, have an unemployment rate that is easily ten times the national average. The Senate report on poverty discovered that nearly half the status Indians in Canada at the time were unemployed. There are few jobs to be lost because so few of the people whom I represent have been unable to get worthwhile jobs either from the government or from the resource corporations that have lately become so interested in the north.
Restraints on government spending are nothing new for the north or for native people in general. It has never been

any other way. I would like to know just how much of the Indian Affairs program budget of some $366 million this year will actually reach native people in a form which is useful to them. I have a feeling it will not be very much. It is time this government stopped overlooking these people. It is time the government stopped looking at native land claims as a nuisance and starting looking at them as an opportunity to provide the original inhabitants of this country with a decent standard of life, with dignity. It is time for imaginative and bold measures to give the north some measure of self-government. It is time for the government to provide the funds and the training so that northern poeple can become full members of this country, of this just society.
This country will face huge problems in the years ahead. The problem with the resource corporations which want to take all the wealth out of the north without putting anything back is one that all Canadians have had and will continue to have, as I and other members of my party have pointed out many times. The task of providing everyone in the country with a decent standard of life, with dignity, has not yet been carried out. The problem of northerners and of native people in general is only the most extreme example of a problem that all ordinary Canadians have when they confront a system that values profits more highly than people. In solving it for these people, we may learn how to solve it for all Canadians.
The people of whom I have just spoken need assurance that they will share equally in the nation's progress in the years to come. I am disappointed that the government did not see fit to give such assurance in its throne speech. The problems of which I have spoken may not be the only problems the government will face in the coming months and years, but they are among the most serious. There are three important areas of concern for the north. I hope hon. members will bear them in mind, study them and try to find ways of solving our problems. I refer to providing more responsible government for the Northwest Territories, more representation in terms of two members from the Northwest Territories and, of prime importance, the problems of native people all across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin by congratulating you and your deputies upon your appointments. I am confident you will carry out your responsibilities with skill and distinction in the great tradition of your predecessor. I also wish to congratulate the mover and the seconder on their remarks, remarks which demonstrated their ability and indicated the promise of future achievement.
I am understandably pleased that the Speech from the Throne carries forward much of my work as minister of consumer and corporate affairs. The speech proposes the reintroduction of the first stage combines bill amendments, the Canada Business Corporations Act and its Canadian director provisions,, and the anti-profiteering legislation, all of which I presented to the House during the last parliament. The speech also mentions a comprehensive overhaul of consumer credit legislation, total revision of our bankruptcy law, improved safety of consumer electrical products, and the establishment of more consumer storefront offices. All these are measures involve initiatives which I took, work which I did and which I
October 10, 1974

announced prior to July 8. These measures are important to the well-being of all Canadians as consumers. I believe these were among the measures Canadian voters had in mind when they gave the government such a strong vote of confidence on election day.
The government, in the throne speech, identifies inflation as Canada's most serious problem and says "it is necessary to both deal with its causes and mitigate its effects". There is as yet no clearcut final consensus among economists today as to the causes of inflation, nor of the best way to achieve its cure. But increasingly economists are saying that it is wrong to rely solely on macro-economic policies, broad brush policies involving monetary and fiscal measures affecting the entire economy in a general way. Instead, they say that more attention must be paid to micro-economic matters, to particular situations in the economy as well as to its general operation. In other words, they say there are structural problems in the Canadian and world economy lying behind many of the upward pressures on prices that we have seen in our country.
They argue that concentrations of economic power may well be able to achieve higher prices for their products and pass these prices on to the rest of the economy, free from the total pressures of the marketplace. These prices would then, in turn, help bring about price increases in other goods and services, and on and on in the inflationary spiral. While monetary and fiscal policies may ultimately be able to deal with these effects of concentrations of economic power, this could well be a lengthy process and in the meantime the impact of these general policies could bring about a disastrous slowdown to the economy as a whole.
If it is the case, as I think it is, that structural rigidities are among the important causes of today's inflation, then the government must have available to it the means to strike at them directly instead of relying solely on monetary and fiscal policies. Certainly, with the evidence we have of economic stagnation in Canada today, we should not take the risk of relying solely on these policies whose impact against inflation is primarily to slow down the entire economy. This is why I believe the government must have the stage one competition policy bill and the anti-profiteering bill among its primary weapons in its fight against inflation. They must be given very high legislative priority to ensure that their benefits will be available to Canadians as soon as possible.
I recognized that the time available to the House before Christmas for the consideration of legislation is limited. This is because of the time required for the debate on the Speech from the Throne and on the budget and for dealing with estimates. I understand that the government, therefore, intends to present only a small number of rather technical bills which are necessary to increase lending limits under certain programs such as that of the Export Development Corporation. Unless these bills are passed, the programs would cease to function. There is also the bill to increase veterans' benefits. But none of these measures is highly controversial. Surely it should, and must, be possible for the House leaders to negotiate limits to debate
The Address-Mr. Gray
on them so that all these bills could go through the House in a very few days.
The result would be that the House could move immediately thereafter-and before Christmas-to the first stage competition bill and the anti-profiteering legislation. The first stage bill received second reading, that is, approval in principle, from the House and was well into consideration by the finance committee when the election came. At that time I had already submitted to the finance committee a series of amendments aimed at dealing with many of the valid points raised in public and parliamentary debate on the bill up to that point. I would, therefore, urge that the House agree to give the first stage competition bill second reading without another full second reading debate and refer it immediately to the finance committee so that its consideration could continue from the point at which the committee left off before election day.
If it is important to the fight against inflation that the first stage competition bill should become law as soon as possible, I believe it is equally important for the government to make the necessary policy decisions and present to the House, also as soon as possible, a bill to implement the second stage of the new competition policy. The first stage bill, which was given first reading last week, is identical to the one I presented before the election. That bill proposed strengthening the law against misleading advertising and giving new consumer protection in the field of warranties and guarantees as well as against certain undesirable selling practices. Also, it would give the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission new civil jurisdiction to make orders against practices such as refusal to deal which could have adverse effects on competition.
The bill would make it easier for the courts to find, on the facts, that there had been unlawful combinations in restraint of trade. It would extend the Combines Investigation Act generally to apply to the field of services. It would authorize higher penalties by the courts, both in terms of fines and imprisonment, for those convicted of offences against the act. In addition, for the first time it would give those injured by breaches of the act the right to sue for civil damages. These are all important and necessary steps in improving our competition law so that it would do more to help competitive pressures work more actively against rising prices in the economy.
The government decided during the last parliament that other possible changes in the anti-trust law pertaining to mergers, monopolies and specialization agreements would be dealt with in the second stage of legislative consideration. But these aspects, also, are highly relevant to dealing with the structural causes of inflation. I believe it is essential, therefore, that the second stage bill be produced without delay.
In my view, it should not be necessary for a further round of formal consultations with business and other groups to take place before the government makes up its mind as to the contents of the bill. After all, the process of review of competition policy has been going on since 1966 when the government referred the matter to the Economic Council for study and recommendation. The council issued its report in 1969. There was much public debate on the

October 10, 1974
The Address-Mr. Gray
contents of the report, as there was was after the first competition bill was presented in 1971.
A series of seminars was held by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in 1972 as a means of further consultation with business and other groups on all aspects of competition policy. Then there was the public and parliamentary debate when I presented the stage one bill to parliament in the fall of 1973. During all this period, briefs and recommendations were submitted to the government by interested groups. I believe, therefore, that the government is now in a position to make decisions as to the contents of the second stage bill. I believe that now is the time for decision and action on the bills covering both stages of legislative reform. There would still be ample opportunity for the views of all interested groups and individuals on the proposals in the second stage bill to be considered as it proceeded through the parliamentary process, especially during the committee stage.
I think the Speech from the Throne should also have made reference to plans by the government to present the second stage competition bill. The Speech from the Throne which we are considering announces the welcome decision by the government to extend the life of the Food Prices Review Board to the end of 1975. By this expression of confidence, the government confirms the credibility and degree of achievement I forecast the board would develop when I was speaking out in support of, and in defence of, the board here in the House and before the media during its first months of activity. However, in announcing the decision to extend the board's life to December, 1975, the Speech from the Throne is marked by what I consider to be a serious omission. If this omission represents the government's intentions, it means the board will lose much of its hard-won credibility and usefulness.
The Speech from the Throne says the board's mandate will be renewed "so that it may continue to report regularly on trends in food prices and analyse the reasons for price changes in specific areas." But these are only two of the three important terms of reference under which the board is presently operating. The third is that in reporting its findings it can make recommendations for action by the government and by the private sector. It was by virtue of this authority that it was able to make recommendations for the subsidy programs which have been helping to restrain increases in the prices of bread and milk. I shall have more to say about the milk subsidy in a few moments. This authority also helped make it possible for the board to recommend that action be taken in respect of what it found to be unwarranted increases in bread prices late last February.
As the House will recall, on the basis of these findings I personally intervened and was able to get the bakery industry to roll back bread prices to levels which the board found acceptable, levels which generally prevailed until the recently announced increases. These are increases about which, I might say, no one in government has so far had anything to say. I would call attention, also, to the board's recommendations for action with respect to egg marketing, recommendations which helped the government decide to begin dealing with that deteriorating situation.
To continue its present and growing usefulness, the board must be able to go on making recommendations for action and to report its findings of fact and its recommendations directly to the public as it does at the present time. To take away this authority would make the renewal of the board's mandate largely meaningless. The government should indicate without delay its commitment to letting the board continue to exercise this authority to make recommendations for government and private action.
The government has rightly said in the Speech from the Throne that it does not intend "to deliberately generate slack in the economy in order to combat inflation." I think this means that parliament, and Canadians generally, must be vigilant to ensure that the government does not bring about such a result unintentionally rather than deliberately as an inadvertent side effect of measures whose ostensible purposes are quite different. Along with inflation there are disturbing signs of slowdown, of recession in the economy. Great care must be taken by the government not to do things which would precipitate the economy into deeper recession, or worse, in view of what this would obviously mean in terms of high unemployment and harm, particularly for the less fortunate groups in our economy.
There must be an equitable sharing of the burdens of dealing with inflation. These burdens must not be thrown disproportionately on the shoulders of the working people and small business people of our country. Of course, the government has said in the throne speech no one group should shoulder an unfair burden. This statement is one which we all welcome. However, the test of the government's effectiveness in reaching this objective lies in what is actually happening now and what will be happening over the coming months.
The government has said it will "exercise restraint in its own expenditures with particular emphasis on improving effectiveness and efficiency in existing operations." But frankly, when it comes to restraining government expenditures, I do not believe that the subsidy on fluid milk was the place to start. And yet we had an announcement last August that this subsidy to help restrain increases in the price of milk would be phased out over the next few months. I do not think that this step is consistent with a fair sharing of the burdens of inflation. It is one which will inevitably bring about a sizeable increase in the price of milk, a basic food so important to Canadian children. And the burden of this increase will fall primarily on lower income families, who pay a higher proportion of their incomes for food than other Canadian families.
The Food Prices Review Board has urged that this decision be changed. As the board said in its September 24 statement, "to withdraw the five-cent subsidy in the present circumstances and to do so over a scant four-month period appears to the board to impose an undesirably heavy burden on the Canadian consumer-In these circumstances, the board calls on government to take measures to moderate the rapid fluid milk price increases facing Canadians." The Food Prices Review Board made that statement on September 24, but no one in the government has as yet spoken out in support of this sensible and humane recommendation of the board.

October 10, 1974

It has been argued that increases in family allowances and other social benefits, and their indexing, will make up for the ending of this subsidy. But the government did not cancel the subsidy when it put into effect the increased family allowances and indexing schemes early in 1974. I believe the government should reverse its decision to eliminate the milk subsidy and, as the Food Prices Review Board said, "allow it to continue in the absence of discernible progress in the development of a long-term national dairy policy in view of the other food price increases which consumers currently face." So I hope there will soon be an announcement, in the interests of Canadian children and Canadian families, that the milk subsidy will not be cancelled.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In the throne speech the government has said, as it has said many times in the past, that higher production will be the way we will achieve, if not lower prices or stable prices, at least, as the speech puts it, "the slowing down of price advances." But this can be so only if an increased supply of goods is allowed by the government to exert downward pressures on prices. Increasing the supply of goods and services will do little, if anything, to lower prices if suppliers, because of their economic power, can keep their prices at the same level or even increase them. Increasing supply will not bring about lower prices if government policy itself serves to maintain prices, even when supply increases, or if government policy ratchets them even higher with each increase in the level of supply.
The American economist, Henrik Houthaker, has proposed an urgent examination of all his federal government's regulations and programs to see if they are in fact helping keep prices up. He presented a list of 45 such programs that may be having this effect in the United States. I am sure we could easily develop a similar list in Canada. We should carry out this kind of review in our country and the government should take action, in light of it, on an urgent basis.
Speaking about this kind of approach, another American economist, Gardner Ackley, has said that "this means a concerted attack on structural rigidities in our economy and an energetic effort to dismantle the many institutional, largely governmental, arrangements which raise particular costs and prices." As I said earlier in my remarks, we must make efforts to remove structural rigidities that contribute to inflation. The increasing of flexibility and of competitive pressures in our economy is a key micro-economic way of dealing with our inflation problems. I have already referred to the need in this context to move speedily to implement a reformed and tougher competition policy as well as the anti-profiteering legislation.
Another area which also requires urgent attention is our evolving national farm products marketing system. The will of parliament, as expressed in section 22 of the Farm Products Marketing Act, is that agencies set up under it are "to have due regard to the interests of producers and consumers." However, the recent reports of the Food Prices Review Board on egg marketing indicate that this direction from parliament is not being followed by at least the first of the farm product marketing agencies set up under that act, since CEMA appears up to now to have
The Address-Mr. Gray
been geared to operate primarily in the producers' interest, to increase returns to them and to inhibit the benefits of increased production from being passed on to consumers in the form of lower prices.
Last week the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) announced the government would be appointing additional members to the Farm Products Marketing Council. These members, he said, would not represent the producer interest but instead would be linked with consumers, business and labour. This announcement is welcome. In fact, it is long overdue. This is action I have long advocated and pressed for. The political atmosphere created in very recent weeks by the disclosure of the tragic and wasteful destruction of 28 million eggs finally gave the cabinet the will to take this kind of decision. But welcome as this step is, its true value for consumers should be kept in perspective. Producers will still make up the majority of members on the Farm Products Marketing Council and, in fact, this is required by the National Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. The role of the council itself is very limited; it is to make recommendations to the Minister of Agriculture on whether national marketing agencies should be set up by the federal government. Also it reports to the Minister of Agriculture on their operation once they are created. But the real decisions on the supply and price of a commodity covered by a national marketing agency are made by the members of that agency. This is where the real power lies at present.
Nothing whatsoever has as yet been said by the government about any formal government decision to appoint consumer representatives to national marketing agencies as distinct from the Farm Products Marketing Council. With respect to provincial marketing agencies, I recognize it would be a lengthy and difficult task for the federal government to convince provincial governments to appoint consumer representatives to all provincial marketing boards. But this is an effort the government must also begin.
However, it is quite a different matter when it comes to the national agencies or boards set up by the federal governor in council by proclamation under the Farm Products Marketing Act. The act provides that the governor in council can designate the members of these agencies by proclamation. The act does provide that a majority of members of these agencies must be producers. But, in any event, I believe the government should proceed as quickly as possible to appoint consumer representatives to existing national marketing agencies. It should also state its commitment to appoint consumer representatives to any national agencies that may be created in future. All these appointments should be in sufficient numbers so that they can have a real impact on the decision-making by these agencies, and this means a commitment to amending the act, where necessary, to achieve this purpose.
If all this is not done, the gesture announced by the Minister of Agriculture last week will be largely without meaning. The Windsor Star of September 24, reported that Gordon Hill, president of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, said that "he felt it would only be fair to let a consumer spokesman sit on the Ontario Farm Products Marketing Board and on the federal government's National Farm Products Marketing Council. One vote on the

October 10, 1974
The Address-Mr. Gray
regulatory boards would not swing much weight, he added, but it might give consumers a better insight into what goes on in the marketing of products." However, what is required is not simply a means of giving consumers a better insight into farm products marketing. Instead, they must in fact swing sufficient weight for them to play a meaningful role in decision-making. This can only come from proper representation of consumer and other nonproducer interests on the farm products marketing agencies themselves, and not just on the Farm Products Marketing Council.
The appointment of consumers to these agencies is not an unwarranted intrusion into the private business of farming. Many farmers may not be willing to admit it, but marketing boards and agencies are a form of monopoly or a form of combination in restraint of trade. They fix prices, they regulate supply and they allocate markets. The members of these boards and the farmers dealing with them would, therefore, be subject to investigation and possible prosecution under the combines law if it were not for the clause in the Farm Products Marketing Act specifically excluding such national agencies from the impact of the combines act, our anti-trust law.
In other words, farmers could not lawfully organize their production through national marketing schemes without the authorization of the people of Canada generally, as given through parliament when it passed the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. When parliament did this, the Canadian people in effect authorized the government to set up bodies which are forms of monopolies or combines in restraint of trade. It follows, therefore, that the Canadian people must have an adequate means of ensuring that such bodies operate in the interests not just of one group but of all groups in Canada through the right kind of public supervision and regulation.
I believe that supply-management programs, if properly run and if constructed to operate in a way that balances the interests of farmers and consumers, can be essential in dealing with and stabilizing the food price situation in Canada. The recent disclosures about CEMA have shown what can go wrong with national marketing schemes. Fortunately, this knowledge has come early in the creation of national marketing agencies. Now is the time to appoint consumer representatives in sufficient number to ensure that both consumer and producer interests are taken into account in the decisions of these agencies. Now is also the time to review and amend the National Farm Products Marketing Act and other legislation where necessary to ensure that, in the words of the throne speech of last February, "guarantees against unduly low prices to producers must be coupled with guarantees against unduly high prices to consumers". These words, which I have quoted verbatim from the throne speech, unfortunately did not appear again in the present speech. I believe, therefore, that there should be a renewed public commitment by the government to this objective before this debate ends.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, let me say that the Canadian people, in giving the government a majority mandate on July 8, did so in the expectation of meaningful action on inflation and other problems that confront us. They expect

that the words of the throne speech will be translated into that kind of action as quickly as possible. In voting, they said they wanted a government that was Liberal not only in name but also liberal when it came to both policy orientation and action in terms of concern for people, of ongoing economic and social reform and of strengthening Canadian economic and cultural independence. When Canadian voters gave the government a majority on July 8, they were not simply challenging the government to show what it could do; they were saying, instead, that they expected a definite commitment from the government-a commitment to action, not acting, and a commitment to results, not rhetoric.
It is up to all members of this House of Commons, but especially to those on the government side, to see that the carrying out of this commitment in this positive way is in fact what happens, particularly during this first session and also throughout the entire life of this thirtieth parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I have the pleasure of joining those who spoke before me to offer my congratulations to the movers of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne who acquitted themselves magnificently.
I would also like to congratulate the hon. leader of the House who was named to preside over our deliberations, a difficult task that he kindly accepted to see that parliamentary impartiality is respected both at the level of political parties and official languages.
It is with pride and joy that we can express ourselves in French and in English in a Parliament which always respects the established customs.
We hope that this freedom of expression in the two official languages will be respected from coast to coast so that each Canadian may feel at home everywhere in his country.
We also hope that this fair play will be felt more and more, not only in the official languages area, but also in the distribution of those goods which are essential to life, the natural goods which do not come to us from France or England, but directly from our national production so that all the most elementary needs of each citizen might be satisfied.
The first aim of the Parliament of Canada is to ensure the reign of distributory justice for all citizens of all classes. It is on this essential point that I would like to draw the attention of all the ministers and members of Parliament who were elected or re-elected during the last general election.
Mr. Speaker, I am very optimistic when confronted with life's obligations and I have always managed to face the economic problems of my family. However, I cannot help but see how my fellow Canadians in the riding of Rimouski and the rest of Canada lack the money or the purchasing power which would allow them to adequately participate in the riches of our country and the production of all working Canadians.
I am saddened by this and I am still seeking means to alleviate this tragic situation. To this end, I dared become
October 10, 1974

a member of the Parliament of Canada, with the belief that there lied the supreme authority of the country, where it would be possible to proceed to an adequate and just distribution of this country's wealth and production. I want my right to speak to be recognized and I insist on being taken seriously, especially when I speak of national product and of a better distribution among Canadians.
I see that this Parliament is composed of 57 new members and that 207 members or ministers belonged to the last Parliament. I also note that the former minority Liberal government has been returned to power with a majority sufficient to take its responsibilities without blaming its numerical weakness for its shortcomings. If it cannot settle the problems of Canada, it will only be because of the weakness of its aptitudes or of its character, or because it does not know its obligations and duties.
I am afraid the 57 new members will be as surprised as I was in the last few years at the uselessness of their presence, or their efforts here in Parliament.
Already in the Speech from the Throne and the speech of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), I see to what extent the international or world-wise character of inflation is being used as an excuse not to introduce decent reforms towards a fairer redistribution of the national product among all Canadians.
Instead of continuing to talk about inflation, unemployment and poverty, three of the main consequences of the poor distribution of income, work or purchasing power, why could we not, together, look at the magnificent results of the Canadian production in 1974, which reached $137 billion, that is $6,000 per citizen. If that is so, why do we not all live in affluence or at least in relative comfort?
Why is it that 22.5 million Canadian citizens, with an average per capita income of $6,000, are not satisfied with this production and that the people mainly responsible for the economy are always talking about the need to further increase this production? Have not the members of Parliament themselves asked this same question to the present ministers? It is not enough to produce what we need. We must also ensure a better distribution of this production and this is the responsibility of Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, even though our economy is very dependent upon our relations with foreign countries, far and near, our whole income and tax policy is the business of members of Parliament alone. No citizen of another country, whether from Rome, Paris, London or Washington, has the right to come and solve our problems in matters of family allowances, old age pensions or guaranteed personal incomes, in other words to interfere in business which concerns Canadians only from the moment of their birth to the day of their death. It is therefore in this House, on behalf of all the voters in each constituency, on behalf of all Canadian citizens, that we can best organize the distribution of income and taxes so that we may restore the economic balance between all Canadian citizens and eliminate inflation, unemployment and poverty, thanks to our great national product of $137 billion.
This, Mr. Speaker, is our most important work and responsibility, in other words, it is our only problem. We can consider our impressive national product-without
The Address-Mr. Allard
thinking about inflation, unemployment, poverty. We must be careful not to let ourselves be conditioned by our old habits of considering the economic problems of distribution instead of considering the situation with a new approach, as the 57 new members will probably do. We shall perhaps then be able to find a solution to inflation, poverty and unemployment. If all Canadians enjoy an adequate purchasing power, if all production sells better and more, and the needs of each and everyone are met, then certainly in all areas, towns or parishes, all businesses will be more flourishing, all goods will find buyers, and all production of all goods and services will bring back all available unemployed everywhere.
Let us not blame anyone for the past. There is no use in it. Let us take a good look at the present. Let us know better our present situation and let us look at it as it is without letting ourselves be intimidated by past patters, and I am convinced we will have good surprises.
The right hon. Prime Minister seems to have lofty views about bringing home the constitution of Canada, about drafting a new constitution. Let us wish him every success in this endeavour which may be called for; but what is most important is not changes in the constitution but changes in the distribution of our production for the well being of all Canadians. Let us deal with the first, and then it will be easier, or perhaps unnecessary, to amend the constitution.
One thing remains certain, we can better distribute what we currently produce, and nothing in the constitution steps us from making a proper and fair distribution of incomes and taxes. Everything is there. Let us look at all the powers the government has under the present constitution.
Let us go over section 91 of the BNA Act and take good note of the following subsections stating that the federal government has all powers concerning trade and exchanges, the raising of public money through all modes of taxation, currency, monetary exchanges and coinage, banks and issue of paper money, and interest rates. I am referring to subsections (2), (3), (14), (15) and (19) of section 91 of the BNA Act.
Even if the earth and all the universe have existed for billions of years, even if manking has lived here for several thousand years it was only a few centuries ago that banks, monetary systems, forms of money, capital and credit as means of exchange were created. And money is continually taking new forms.
The monetary, credit, capital, banking and exchange systems, the national and multinational companies are all man-made institutions which must facilitate the lives of men within society, the exchange of goods, products and services which all are based on natural resources.
Mr. Speaker, it is not our debates-for we debate much too much-but our laws which must be blessed by the Almighty, Who may be talking to us through the mouths and pens of our greatest businessmen who are personally concerned about inflation.
The illness has reached its culminating point. Now, the big guns are thundering. It is no longer economists or university professors who are talking, but two of the highest administrators of our million-rich banks and com-

October 10, 1974
The Address-Mr. Allard
panies who are dealing with their shareholders as chairmen of the Royal Bank of Canada and the Bank of Montreal respectively, at the end of the financial year on October 31, 1973. The reference is exact and the documents in question are available at any branch of both these banks.
Let us be glad that these men are finally impressed by this everlasting situation of inflation, unemployment and poverty and that they sould request from the government the political rectifications necessary to restore national economic balance between all regions of our prosperous Canada. Everybody can find there most valuable advice.
Here are a few passages from the speech delivered by Mr. G. Arnold Hart, chairman of the Bank of Montreal, but the whole speech should be studied, it is as if it were directed to us, in this House. I quote:
There is no doubt that our economy is still corroded by inflation and it is increasingly urgent to heal it as times goes by.
All of us are collectively responsible in some way or other. But this question overrides the interests of all groups in our society; and neither capital, nor labour nor any single interest group, good as its organization may be, has the capacity and the responsibility for taking an overall view of the situation.
Only the state can do this and it alone has the responsibility for doing so.
Canadians generally want all members in the community to benefit from a higher living standard and quality of life made possible by economic achievements of this great country of ours.
I know Canadians will be ready to take up the challenge if the problem is put forward to them frankly.
The time has come for fundamental alteratives.
Will our elected representatives become aware of it?
This is talking frankly and sincerely!
Here now a few excerpts from the speech of Royal Bank of Canada Chairman Earle McLaughlin, administrator almighty.
We tried to outline the vital links between the bank and the society it serves.
Not only do economic disparities have an economic impact, they also frequently have painful human repercussions.
Those are real problems as people live them in their bodies and their souls. Thus, the rate of unemployment and the average per capita income are empty abstractions which do not bear witness to the ordeal of the jobless father trying to find the means to provide for his family.
We are one of the wealthiest countries in the world nowadays, and we enjoy an envied rate of living and prosperity.
Our national economic prosperity seems to dig ever wider the gap between "have" and "have not" areas.
The problem of economic disparities however conceals human situations that are too outrageous to be born simply with resignation.
National economic development is more than a simple matter of statistics and national gross product. It urgently calls for an orderly redistribution of the fruit of prosperity throughout the country.
How indeed could we take pride in our general economic growth if many of our fellow citizens do not get a fair share of that prosperity?
It seems that the most advantageous approach to regional disparities would be to consider the problem in a national context and not at the regional level.
This is speaking frankly and sincerely!
As we can see, the appeal comes from high authority, and it is the government of Canada that is called on to take action having full authority to plan our economy.

Mr. Speaker, the chairmen of the two largest banks in Canada who are also serving as directors of the largest multimillionaire companies, must know a few things about the administration of our country. They are calling on the government to take decisive and efficient action in reestablishing the national economic balance between all Canadian citizens, thus removing at the same time inflation, unemployment and poverty.
Those are the major principles on which is based a total policy dictated to us by the most influential Canadians, a policy desired by all Canadians. The government is called upon to take action and we, in the opposition, are prepared to support it along this line.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a great day in my life. For 15 years I have wanted to serve as a member of the House of Commons. I grant you that my reasons over the 15 years have changed, but my enthusiasm certainly has not. I consider that being a member of this House is an honourable profession. As a matter of fact, the member who has brought to this House the most honour, certainly in my lifetime, has been the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). So today I pay him tribute. It would be remiss of me not to mention another hon. member who for the past four years represented the riding of Selkirk, namely, Doug Rowland. Although he is not in the same political party as I am, he is an honest man and one of whom we were proud when he was a member of parliament.
Today I will deal with two basic areas. First, I wish to address some remarks on a more philosophical basis regarding the direction in which I think this government should be going. Second, I will tell you a story of a great naval battle which took place on the prairies. No doubt this will be of particular interest to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. Finally, I will be much more parochial and will speak about Selkirk in particular.
Every member of parliament works from a basically philosophical principle-a pivotal point. My pivot centres around Biblical principles. I believe there are certain basic principles that are morally right, and certain that are morally wrong. I think that this government, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in particular, would be well advised to give some heed to those Biblical principles which are as applicable today to modern man as they have ever been. In particular, sir, I think it would be well for this government to realize that in Canada it is not the government that is sovereign, nor is the Queen or the Crown. In fact, we must go back to the sovereignty of God.
I point out to this government that it should give some measure of tribute, however small and insignificant it may be, to those basic scriptural principles on which our civilization was built. Furthermore, I think that this government would do well to understand that the government should rule from a principle of justice, not from a principle of power. I feel that the Prime Minister and his cabinet have not yet come to grips with this principle and have not made the choice between government by power and government by justice, even though they have used that
October 10, 1974

hollow phrase "the just society" since 1968. I think that this government would be well advised to agree that we should be the world leaders in establishing a massive development program, because if we are to consider justice for Canadians we cannot really apply justice in Canada unless we are prepared to do it in an honest way.
We should all agree that justice extends beyond our national boundaries to every man on the face of the earth. In terms of both our reserves and our natural resources, we probably can be considered one of the richest nations in the world. For us to think always in terms of nationalistic policy is both naive and provincial. I do not think the government can be commended for its infantile approach to this matter, as demonstrated by the fact that the CIDA program amounts to a commitment to world development of only 1 per cent of our gross national product. I wish also to warn the government and caution them against adopting an attitude of economic assimilation of other countries, believing that somehow these other countries should mould themselves to our viewpoint with regard to their economic development. I do not think the government would be well advised to take an ethnocentric development perspective. Rather, we should understand that perhaps other countries, although not developed to the same degree as we are, nevertheless on occasion may have stumbled upon some element of truth.
I should like to speak more on these basic philosophical principles but I want to leave myself enough time to refer to matters which pertain to the Selkirk riding. Therefore, I will now go into story time. I remember very well a morning early in May. I arose and the sun was shining as it usually does in Manitoba. A warm, gentle wind was blowing. As I walked out of my apartment on to the sidewalk, I found some alarm among the people there. The cry I heard was "The Liberals are coming, the Liberals are coming". You know, Mr. Speaker, Manitoba is very flat and that is why we have a great perspective; we can see a long way out.
I remember looking to the east into the distance and seeing this great Liberal armada making its way through the prairies. As it came closer, I noticed a great flagship and on the ship was Admiral Trudeau. On his right I saw a most impressive battleship on which was Rear-Admiral Richardson, or maybe I should say Rear-Rear-Rear-Rear-Admiral Richardson. On the left side of the ship was an aircraft carrier laden with 707 airplanes bound for the port of Winnipeg. There was some suggestion that perhaps there were some Air Canada planes on that ship as well. In total, there were some 45 most impressive ships in the fleet, with banners waving in the western wind.
I want to be honest in relating this story, so I must tell you that to meet this great fleet was but a small task force of loyal westerners, two Manitobans. That in itself would not have been bad, were we not facing a war on two fronts, because it seemed that over the previous 18 months the Liberals had allies and were coming from the rear with land forces. Now I want to dispose of the third party in the war, Mr. Speaker. As I remember, as the battle progressed this third element was somewhat confused and in disarray, not knowing whether they were fighting us or the oncoming Liberal fleet. What happened to that third force is well known on the prairies.
The Address-Mr. Whiteway
As I led my very small task force in Selkirk to meet this great fleet, I remembered the legend of a battleship which was tied up at the port of Prince Albert and allegedly was due to join the mothball fleet. With all the reserves I could muster, I called upon this great battleship of Prince Albert, and it was ready. Mr. Speaker, when a volley of shots came from this mighty Prince Albert battleship it hit that Liberal fleet with deadly accuracy and it hit Prime Minister with the sting of a thousand hornets.
In the early stages of this great battle it became very apparent to Rear-Admiral Richardson that he was losing, so he decided to call out the reserves from Halifax. It would seem that there were ships ready to go, but no crews to man them. Mr. Speaker, if the civil service were sailors, there would not be enough ships in the entire Dominion of Canada to accommodate them. Those ships were without a crew and could not come to the aid of the minister. This battle waged fiercely. It was an awesome battle for some eight weeks. When the smoke cleared late in the evening of July 8, the Liberal fleet had been sunk on the prairies and Rear-Admiral Richardson's ship was listing heavily to the left. There were only five survivors. Lieutenant-Colonel Lang was directing survival operations, encouraging the five men who were desperately clinging to a life-raft. Sir, that is a true story.

Their condition probably would not have been conducive of consumption, Mr. Speaker. For the next few minutes I should like to speak about the riding of Selkirk. The great philosopher, Mr. John Locke, once said that a man could not be converted by a one-time brilliant argument. My role is not to convert the Prime Minister, but to be a depth-sounder. Anyone from the maritimes or who has travelled the oceans will know what a depth-sounder is. It is an instrument that sends an electronic wave to the bottom of the sea; the wave then bounces back and is measured, and from that they can tell how deep the water

October 10, 1974
The Address-Mr. Whiteway
is. Depth of water is usually measured in fathoms, which is about the span of an average man's arms, about six feet. I believe my role is to be a depth-sounder for the government of this country, to measure the depth of water for the ship of state in western Canada. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, if some government policies were a popsicle stick they would go aground in western Canada.
As a mere deckhand, I would not in my wildest moments of imagination even remotely consider advising the captain, the Prime Minister, as to the course his great ship of state should take in the west. But one thing I can do: I can watch diligently for the west and I can point out the reefs and the rocks, and I can tell the captain when the ship is nearing the shore. I may mention some towns that the Prime Minister and the government have never heard of, but I will take that chance. I might even have the honour of having the Prime Minister's eyes, even for a fleeting moment, look at the words that I speak today as they will appear in Hansard. There is in the Selkirk riding a town by the name of Gimli. Former ministers of defence know Gimli well, because they took from it an air force base that was vital to its survival. Only through the intestinal fortitude of the Vikings of Gimli, the town survived in spite of the federal government.
In Gimli there is a firm called Saunders Aircraft. I will not comment on whether it is a particularly viable industry at the present time. I am not one of those trigger-happy politicians who is willing to take a shot at Saunders Aircraft for any reason, but I will say that this Liberal government should extend the same kind of aid to it as is being given to eastern aircraft companies. The government should show us the formula they used in deciding the kind of subsidies and grants given to aircraft companies, so that we can understand their reasoning with respect to Saunders. They have recently paid token appreciation to the company's attempts to establish a viable industry in the town.
Some 15 years ago, the federal government-I must say it was not a Liberal government-built a great breakwater in Gimli but made no provision for its maintenance. Fifteen years later that breakwater is shifting. It is certainly inadequate in its present condition. I know that to some degree the government of Manitoba must assume responsibility because they raised the level of the lake two feet more than its level when the breakwater was built. However, we will not solve the problem by simply passing the buck and saying it is not the fault of the federal government that the water is rising. The fact is that the water has risen by two feet, the breakwater is inadequate and the town is in trouble. That is not the only deep water there is in Manitoba for this government.
Moving southerly down the lake from Gimli, we come to Sandy Hook. Counting all the dogs, cats and other living matter, I suppose the population of Sandy Hook is not in excess of 85 or 90 people. I could continue and speak about the city of Winnipeg, a large portion of which lies within Selkirk constituency. However, my time is running out and I want to bring to light a matter which I mentioned very briefly. It concerns work. I believe that in western Canada there are jobs for most Canadians who really want to work. We in western Canada believe in the work ethic. This country was moulded by people who knew what it was to put in a hard day's work. I do not want to be accused of suggesting overly simplistic solutions. In fact, I am only discussing the problems, not suggesting in-depth solutions. However, I want this government to be aware that the water is very shallow. In western Canada we hear it said that Canadians are being paid $2.2 billion not to work. This government would be well advised to accept the idea that it is better for a man to work at any job than to not work at all. The pendulum has swung far enough to the left. I do not accept the idea that Canadians have a right to the natural resources of this country, if they are not prepared to put any work into them.
I believe in the basic Biblical principle and the basic practical principle that unless a man is prepared by the sweat of his brow or the labour of his mind to put some effort forward, he has not earned the right to any of the rewards which this country can offer.
