speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to be able to congratulate the Speaker on his election. I am especially pleased to do so because we in Northern Ontario are very proud to have the Speaker come from our area. As we are aware, Northern Ontario is the very centre of this country, and of course while the Speaker does not come from the exact centre, since the exact centre is Thunder Bay, he does come from that satellite of Thunder Bay, the city of Sudbury, which is about 700 miles away. I think he has already demonstrated the kind of flexibility, the keen grasp of difficult situations, and sense of humour that bode very well for his work in the future.
I should also like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Duclos) and seconder (Mr. Lee) of the Address in Reply, as well as the other members who have been elected to the very important positions of Deputy Speaker, Deputy Chairman of Committees, and the Assistant Deputy Chairman of Committees, the latter being yourself, Madam Speaker.
To form a government in these times is a most difficult task. It has often been said that it would be much easier to be sitting in opposition at this time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Do you want to trade?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not say that is what I want to do, but I say it is much easier to be there. I think we have to look upon these times as being totally unique.
A great deal has been said about inflation, but we have always had some inflation. We have had rapid inflation in places like China and parts of Europe, and an endemic sort of inflation in South America which has lasted through generations.
Since World War II there has been about 2 per cent or 3 per cent inflation annually. There has been inflation associated with unemployment, which is a peculiarity, and

we ascribe to administered pricing. I do not however think there has been any period in history, except for very short periods, when inflation reached the present level and was sustained at that level. This is inflation which tends to be caused by excessive demand.
I am just using inflation to show how our times are unique, Madam Speaker, but I do not wish to deal with this topic at this time. Since we have not had comparable problems in the past, the traditional attempts to cure them have not worked. I should like to discuss the matter of demand, and study some solution for inflation in terms of doing something about demand, rather than constantly looking at the supply side of the situation.
I agree that we must continue to increase supply, but we must be careful not to create more tense and inflationary situations than we can cure. I should like to examine the demand side in the areas of energy and foods as I think these are extremely important areas and becoming more so all the time.
Before doing that, however, I should like to look at a couple of reasons why demands in energy and food have become almost intolerable. The first reason, I believe, is the relative affluence of the developed countries like Canada and the United States, which has put tremendous pressure on the demand side. This means that supply situations are very difficult to fulfil, and I should like to illustrate that when I speak later about energy.
Certainly the affluent people are consuming a far greater proportion of the world's goods than they did 20 or 30 years ago. I understand that consumption of beef in Canada has increased by about 20 pounds per capita in 12 years. These things create real demand problems.
Another factor is the growing world population. It is increasing by about 2.1 per cent annually; that is 75 million more mouths to feed each year. By the turn of the century the world's population will have doubled. It was something like 3.8 billion in 1970 and will be close to 8 billion by the year 2000 given the present trends, which seem difficult to reverse.
The third factor that contributes to the problem is the fact that more countries are becoming developed, although I do not think this is as large a factor as the two previously mentioned, particularly in the area of food.
I should like to deal with the question of energy now because I think this is one area where we can take action to lessen demand. An article in Oilweek magazine of September 16, 1974, at page 10 quotes Mr. A. E. Pallister, Vice Chairman of the Science Council of Canada, as saying that we must do something about levelling out the demand curve for energy, particularly oil.
He points out that supply curves tend to level off and even decrease under given circumstances. He says that even with the western reserves, the islands and the far north and so on, the supply curves tend to fall short of the demand curves, and even decrease. On the other hand, the demand curve rises steadily and tends to increase its slope through these periods, so that when we get to the mid 1980s where the supply and demand curves cross we will not be able to continue meeting demand.
I think this situation in oil and natural gas applies not only in Canada but throughout the rest of the world. In
October 10, 1974

the case of hydro power we have long passed the stage where supply can be increased substantially. The areas where this can be done are rather limited.
This over emphasis in attempting to meet demand by increasing supply in the energy field is creating some tremendous distortions in our economy and in our environment, as well as tremendous social distortions.
I wish to name one or two of these areas where the distortions are particularly evident. The James Bay project is most disturbing. Parts of the project make sense and may be carried out very easily. However, when we talk about the James Bay project in terms of $10 billion or $12 billion, along with the South Indian Lake project, the proposed Mackenzie Valley Pipeline, and the tar sands investment when we speak about $100 billion of energy investment in the next 10 years, $100 billion, we are talking about creating tremendous problems and a very serious dislocation of our economy. We must ask ourselves whether these projects are worth it? Are there better ways of doing this?
I mentioned the environmental situation. When costing these projects, we must start internalizing some of the external costs. We must internalize the environmental and social costs to the native population.
The South Indian Lake project is not as costly in terms of investment. However, it is very costly in terms of the environment and what it will do to our native people.
There are many things to be taken into consideration. For example, if the James Bay project and several others were being undertaken at the same time with the use of foreign funds, this would distort the picture through increased value of the Canadian dollar. What happens when the Canadian dollar rises to $1.10, $1.15 or $1.20 in terms of an important industry like pulp and paper so sensitive to dollar fluctuation? This is a very important industry in Quebec, northern Ontario, British Columbia and other parts of the country. Industries such as this will suffer with this kind of dislocation.
We must begin rationalizing our efforts to increase supply. Although it is necessary to increase supply naturally, we must look at it very carefully.
I now wish to deal with the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. It appears that perhaps the bottom has fallen out due to the proposition of EL PASSO to run the gas across the Valdez cut. However, it looks as though the oil pipeline will go ahead. The United States government has again mentioned it.

speechtext:
I do not want to get into a long debate on this topic, but I do agree that part of the James Bay project may have some merit as a hydro scheme. However, I also suggest the CANDU reactor type of program has a great deal of merit. I have an interest in this program. It is the kind of thing we should be examining. However, it is a matter of opinion. I feel we should look at alternate ways of doing this.
The Mackenzie Valley oil pipeline is another very large project. It will be a good deal more expensive than the gas project, and much more difficult to engineer by reason of the fact that the oil must be heated to 180 degrees in order to flow through the pipeline. There is also the problem of going through the tundra. There is the very special problem of going through the semi-tundra. Some areas have perma frost, others do not. This will create many problems.
I am very concerned about the Mackenzie Valley situation. A group of members of this House talked to members of the United States congress about a year ago. They indicated they would like this Mackenzie Valley oil pipeline in 1982. I think there is some honesty there.
We have another problem and it is becoming a very dangerous situation. It has to do with the Cherry Point situation. When we talked to the Americans last summer we were assured beyond any doubt that the super tankers that would be plying the waters around the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Cherry Point would be double skinned. There was no question about their being double bottomed. We now find this is not to be the case. These are single skin ships.
On August 29 a Canadian delegation met with the Americans. It is my understanding that this matter was not even raised. We had a commitment that these ships would have double bottoms and there would be other precautions. These precautions are not being taken. It is almost a certainty that a collision will occur, and the whole area around Cherry Point and the islands around Vancouver will be polluted by oil. They will be virtually destroyed environmentally. Situations of this kind must be carefully studied.
I am concerned about ways and means of reducing our demand for all types of energy. This must be done in the most intelligent way possible. For example, we have an office of energy conservation. That office must be given all help possible. We must be prepared to spend money in order to reduce this demand for energy. Money spent in this way would be far more productive than the vast sums

October 10, 1974
The Address-Mr. McRae
of money that will have to be spent if we continue on the path of increasing supply to meet demand.
I wish to spend a moment on the world food situation. Here, increasing supply is all we can do. I well remember sitting in an auditorium in Thunder Bay in the mid sixties when the headmasters of the province of Ontario were being addressed by Dr. Brock Chisholm, a very famous Canadian, and executive director of the World Health Organization. He drew a vivid picture of food problems that would develop in the world in the next 10 to 15 years. He talked about what would happen in the early seventies. His predictions have proven very accurate.
Throughout the sixties there was an increase in food production, not only in the developed world but also the underdeveloped world. However, in 1972, due to a combination of bad weather conditions in various parts of the world and a series of other events, cereal crops were reduced by 33 million tons from a total production of 1200 million tons. In the meantime, while this was going on, 75 million more mouths had to be fed, using 25 additional tons of cereals. So there was a net loss of 58 million tons in 1972. The year 1973 was more favourable but there was still a net loss.
In 1974 the situation may be very grave. There was an extremely wet spring in parts of Canada and the United States, a very dry summer, and an early frost in the fall- the worst possible combination of events. I understand that the crop situation in the U.S.S.R. is also not measuring up to expectations. We find the Sahara desert spreading annually and there is a major famine there.
According to the Canadian Conference on the World Food problem held this week, the world has about 26 days' supply of cereal grains in storage. In other words, if there was a serious stoppage of production of cereal grain, the world could survive 26 days before stocks ran out. A few people are becoming very concerned about the world food situation.

speechtext: You are doing all right!

I admit I am one who should, perhaps, be more concerned personally. Earlier I mentioned the causes which led to the present situation, and they certainly have to do with the relative affluence of a few people like myself and a few others around here.
I think the FAO Conference in Rome in November must be regarded as of extreme importance. Something will have to be done. The papers I have seen for use as a basis for the Rome meeting indicate there will be strong pressure in this direction. Here we find a situation in which we must increase the food supply. One way of doing this is to put more land into production. Another is to prevent our cities eating up rich agricultural land. Another is to increase the production of fertilizer, especially of synthetic fertilizer.
We ought to convert more fuel energy into fertilizer. I believe that today 7.9 per cent of our gasoline and 17 per cent of our diesel fuel is used on farms. Vast amounts of natural gas, particularly, are required in fertilizer production today. It is important that natural gas be used for
[Mr. McRae.)
fertilizer in an effort to increase the world food supply rather than being used in directions which are less important.
We should also show more concern about constructing adequate facilities for food storage. We cannot rest easy with 26 days' supply on hand.

We must increase supply in order to meet increased demand and, in another area, we must do more than we have yet done to discourage population growth. I was not happy with the results which came out of the recent conference on world population. A great deal of thinking needs to go into this. While the world population continues to double every 33 years there is bound to be a continuing shortage of food.
We must increase the food supply, but at the same time we ought to take a careful look at whether increasing demand should be encouraged. I should like to quote from an address given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to the Canadian Conference on Banking in Ottawa on September 16:
I propose to press our view that the best and most effective way to overcome the problem of inflation is through policies aimed at encouraging an increase in output and supply. It is important to moderate demand so as to ensure that output does not press too hard against the physical limits of capacity, which would itself serve to generate inflationary pressures.
That is particularly true in the fuel area.
In the few minutes which are left to me I should like to deal, as is customary on this occasion, with a situation in my own riding, particularly with the transportation facilities at Thunder Bay the part they play in the economic and social life of the country.
If we can picture transportation routes in Canada west of Thunder Bay as being two super highways running almost to Thunder Bay, and Canada east of Thunder Bay as being two village roads running east of Thunder Bay, that is more or less the situation. I will explain it a little further. There is the Trans-Canada Highway. We have two of them with paved shoulders and four lanes in many places running right from Vancouver to the Ontario border, and then we have a country road at the Ontario border, an absolute disgrace, a winding highway with unpaved shoulders. While, this is not what I really wanted to spend time on today, I must say we must do something to improve the Trans-Canada Highway. It is a disgrace. It is time the federal government and the province got together and did something about it.
It is the rail connections I want to talk about because I do not think we all realize the kind of situation we have in this country. We have virtually four lines of rail traffic going into Thunder Bay. We have double trackage on the northern line of the CN, or at least we have two lines running along there. We have a lot of double trackage on the CP west of Thunder Bay coming from the Rockies. We have a line from Sioux Look-out, we have the main line of the CP, and a CN line from Winnipeg through Rainy River. These are all, relatively speaking, good lines, lines built for heavy traffic. I know they are not maintained the way they should be maintained, but that is another story.

Therein lies the importance of the harbour of Thunder Bay. All of the traffic comes from the west and very little flows east by rail. Most of it goes by ship.

speechtext:
I wish to congratulate Mr. Speaker on his election to what I consider to be the most important position of impartiality and justice in this venerable and vital institution, and without being facetious, Madam Speaker, I must say that you are the most attractive Speaker to grace this chair. I hold too in special esteem the Clerks at the table, the backbone of this House, and whose unseen hands in so many ways guide the destiny of the House.
The throne speech pays considerable attention to inflation, a situation in this country that is fast becoming a crisis. Nevertheless the Trudeau government, elected to office with a clear majority on July 8, apparently did not feel the situation sufficiently serious to call parliament into session before September 30. There is something reminiscent of Alice in Wonderland in this attitude of indifference to reality.
It could be said in truth that there is a world wide inflationary situation that affects our economy; but it is less than accurate to say that we can do nothing about it. All of the world's trading nations must do something about world inflation, and soon; each must start by putting its own house in order as far as it can, financially and economically. Regardless of our respective points of view, the problem is squarely before us, and its solution is imperative.
While I have great respect for every committee of this House that deals with the estimates and expenditures of government, and for ministers involved in the preparation of budget estimates, I believe the time has come to take a giant step forward in examining the total impact of gov-
The Address-Mr. Howie
ernment expenditures, and studying new systems and methods that can streamline our operation and lighten the burden on the Canadian taxpayers. As a corollary to this I believe we should examine the impact of government spending on the Canadian economy and its relationship to the inflationary spiral.
Since the royal commission on government organization, commonly called the Glassco Commission, reported in 1962, the $6.5 billion expenditure of that year has tripled in the 12 year interval to some $22 billion, shown in the main estimates before the 29th parliament, and those before this parliament are substantially the same.
In the 12 years since the Glassco Commission reported some outstanding social legislation has been enacted, and federal government assistance to disabled and disadvantaged Canadians has improved immeasurably, both in its quality and amount. Indeed in respect to disabled people, particularly the blind, and in respect to our senior citizens 1 find it easy to support the proposals of my colleagues in this House for even more generous treatment. I personally hope the day will come when the old age pension will no longer be regarded as income for tax purposes.
At the same time I believe we can make some real progress in identifying areas within each department of government which can, and should, provide a service for other departments of government, thus avoiding costly duplication and the tremendous expense of hiring outside professional and other services, and of consulting with experts outside the departments of government.
In department after department of government, estimated expenditures climb. The estimates I referred to earlier show that justice and the administration of our courts had an allocation of $23 million, more than double the previous year's budget. Correctional services were increased by $34 million to $172 million. The RCMP budget increased by $20 million to $125 million. The Food Prices Review Board rose to $1.9 million, up 90 per cent over the previous year. The CBC increased its budgeted expenditures by 25 per cent to $298.8 million. The Post Office went up 17 per cent to $689.7 million. The Commission on Official Languages was up 36 per cent to $1.9 million.
It is imperative that every expenditure receive the closest possible scrutiny, but the time allocated to our House committees to perform this function, and the research facilities needed to dig into it are not sufficient to do the best possible job for the Canadian people. I am sure the ministers of the Crown have done their utmost to cut the fat, and I am confident the opposition will demand every economy; but I feel too that the very essence of our administrative system should also be examined so that, through the combined efforts of all of us, we give the Canadian taxpayer the best break possible.
Our system, despite all its shortcomings, is good, but I think it can be improved. I feel that, considering the tremendous increase in the complexity of government organization since the Glassco Commission of 12 years ago, we need to examine our administrative process in the light of the vast improvements and changes that have taken place in business, accounting, policy auditing, and computerization, and thus ensure that the total delivery system of government best serves the challenge the

October 10, 1974
The Address-Mr. Howie
Canadian people have given us. We need another Glassco type commission now.
Socially and economically rural Canada faces a crisis. The social problems are caused by increased and disastrous depopulation; the economic problems by vulnerable markets and the cost-price squeeze. In my province of New Brunswick, since 1900 approximately 25,000 acres of farmland per year have been lost to agriculture for the purposes of forestry, housing, industrial and commercial development. In 1951 there were 26,431 census farms; in 1971 there were 5,485 census farms in New Brunswick. Rural non-farming inhabitants represent 39 per cent of the population of New Brunswick, a much larger percentage than elsewhere in Canada.
As a major step in revitalizing the agricultural industry I suggest we consider a program to expand the scope and volume of research programs designed to assist agriculture; undertake a comprehensive and sustained program of research into prospective domestic and world market demands for agricultural products, develop and expand secure markets for Canadian agricultural products, and help translate Canada's tremendous agricultural potential into reasonably priced food on the table for Canadians and, indeed, for hungry people throughout the world.
We should also undertake a comprehensive review of transportation requirements to find ways to improve the transport of agricultural products between the regions of Canada and into export position, and to reduce transportation costs to the farmer. We must mount an aggressive campaign to lower world tariffs on farm products, and to overcome other impediments to agricultural exports. We must also design a program to assist farmers to finance the purchase or modernizing of machinery, and to assist in developing a structure of service and community facilities in rural areas.
Each of the Atlantic provinces has developed a very significant livestock and poultry industry, which in New Brunswick alone during 1973 resulted in a farm cash income in excess of $46 million and represented nearly 50 per cent of the total cash income from all farming operations. The farm cash income from poultry, meat and eggs represented nearly 32 per cent of the cash income from all livestock and livestock products, including poultry.
The national policy on feed freight assistance was instituted to assist eastern Canada in producing more food during World War II, and was most successful in achieving this goal. This assistance is of major importance to the poultry and livestock industries in the Atlantic provinces, particularly in view of increasing freight rates and rising costs associated with this area of food production.
Poultry feed must have wheat or corn as the major basic ingredient. Neither of these grains has been grown very successfully in these provinces as yet, and we should be very sure that local grain can and will be grown before freight assistance is reduced. Without freight assistance our livestock and poultry industry, especially hogs and poultry, would be at a great disadvantage in competing even for our own markets against provinces or areas with a shorter rail haul. Wifhout feed freight assistance in New Brunswick we would be in an impossible position.

Recently we have been hearing about becoming self-sufficient in home grown grains. Experience over the years has shown this to be very difficult to achieve. Statistics show that we are subject to three to five crop failures for every good one we enjoy. It is evident that a great deal of work needs to be done to develop new varieties and new techniques before we can even hope to come near being self-sufficient.
At present we produce 30 per cent to 40 per cent of our feed grains and must rely on western Canada for the balance. We have a long way to go before we are nearly self-sufficient enough in feed grains, especially in high energy feed that we must have for poultry feed. Any deterioration in these types of production will result in the loss of many thousands of jobs.
I suggest that realistic assistance to Maritime farmers should include; (1), the expansion of the feed freight assistance program to include all grain, corn, livestock feed protein and phosphates, and that the assistance be indexed to reflect, at all times, the actual and increasing cost of movement; (2) the development of an Atlantic grain program that would include comprehensive handling, drying, storage, marketing and transportation assistance provisions; (3), a crash program to support more extensively research to be conducted in the Mari-times to assist in the development of a hardy species of grain indigenous to Maritime growing conditions and that can be integrated with the potato growing and harvest season; and (4), the development of a system of grain elevators near our ports to purchase and store early in the season a year's supply of needed western grain, to be sold at a constant price throughout the season to Maritime farmers.
I should now like to say a word about our woodlots. In the long run society will derive greater benefits from privately owned woodlots if they are operated by owners who have an interest in their continuing value and yield, rather than be persons who purchase woodlots for cutting rights for the purpose of liquidating the merchantable standing timber in the near future, and who have little or no interest in their other potential value.
Under the rules which currently govern the application of the Income Tax Act, the net returns to an owner-operator of a woodlot are classed and taxed as income. The stumpage value of the trees cut is included. But if a woodlot owner sells cutting rights, called stumpage, to an operator, the proceeds of the sale are classed as the disposal of capital, and only one-half of the increase in value since "V day" is taxable as capital gain. If a woodlot owner has a taxable income, the advantage to him of selling cutting rights, rather than operating the woodlot himself, is obvious.
The operator who purchases cutting rights can claim the cost of the stumpage as an operating cost against the returns from the operation, and the stumpage value is not taxable in his hands. It is true that if an operator-owner can establish a cost base for a woodlot he can claim a capital cost or depletion allowance. However, if the woodlot was purchased several decades ago, or acquired in a way that makes it difficult to establish a cost base, the depletion allowance is likely to be only a small fraction of the stumpage value. There is also the risk that if excessive
October 10, 1974

depletion is claimed, "recaptured depletion" will be taxed as income if and when the property is sold. This provision is less attractive to a woodlot owner than the sale of cutting rights which, as I say, we call stumpage.
The forest resources study in New Brunswick recommends a substantial expansion of the forest extension service, and investment of public funds to encourage more effective operations by woodlot owners. Assessment rolls indicate that there are about 37,000 woodlot owners in New Brunswick, and collectively they own about 25 per cent of the forest land in the province. The percentage of forest land in woodlots is even higher in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.
The discrimination against the woodlot owner-operator should be removed by ruling that the stumpage value of the timber he cuts be regarded as the disposal of capital, and subject to capital gains rules instead of being taxed as income. This would do much to increase production while reducing costs and stabilizing the market.
Let me say a word about tidal power, which has long been advocated by the hon. member for Cumberland-Col-chester North (Mr. Coates). We have a great and immediate problem in this country regarding a most vital situation, a matter which will drastically affect our whole social and economic structure; the energy situation.
Unless the government takes early and appropriate action the Atlantic provinces, which are now starting to narrow the gap of their economic disparity with the rest of the country, will be the section of the country which will particularly receive a severe blow if some long-range and constructive national energy policy is not implemented soon. This is because of the dependence on imported foreign oil for a high percentage of our energy needs at the present time. Yet the Atlantic provinces' region of Canada has within its area some of the greatest energy potentials in the world.
At the head of the Bay of Fundy, between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, the tides rise and fall some 50 feet twice a day, day in and day out, and this phenomenon will go on forever into the future. The magnitude of this tidal range is higher than anywhere else in the world. The volume of water, which regularly and predictably rushes into this unique funnel-shaped topography between our two provinces, amounts to many times the flow of water in the St. Lawrence River. The energy which this volume of water could generate when passing through turbines, amounts to billions of kilowatt hours when converted into electric energy, and in turn represents millions of barrels of oil available every year, and year after year.
The feasibility of tidal power development in the Bay of Fundy was studied and reported upon in 1969 by a board having representation from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and the federal government. I learned from that report that the three sites which were studied in some detail could produce over 87 billion kilowatt hours of electrical energy every year. Some 125 million barrels of oil would be required to generate that amount of electrical energy.
Another analysis contained in the 1969 Tidal Board's Report states that under a double effect scheme of development, 8.7 million kilowatts of installed capacity would generate 17 billion kilowatt hours of energy. The
The Address-Mr. Howie
total capital cost of this scheme was estimated to be some $2 billion, and the estimated energy cost of one site was 5.5 mills per kilowatt hour. The estimate was based upon 7 per cent cost of money, but was compared with oil-fired thermal generation when oil was costing in the vicinity of $1 per barrel.
It is time that the tidal potential of the Atlantic region be actively reviewed and all avenues of innovation implemented. I have discussed the energy potential of the Bay of Fundy tides with engineers who feel that other sites are available which were not studied, even in a preliminary way, by the 1969 board because of the magnitude of the power potential and the corresponding large capital cost. Conditions have changed drastically since 1969 when it was considered prudent not to proceed further with the tidal power concept because of the magnitude of the project, and because at that time oil would produce electrical energy at a slightly cheaper cost.
What a gold mine the Atlantic region and Canada would have today if governments of that day had been less cautious and had proceeded with the construction of this renewable resource and brought it into production!
There must be more positive action taken by government now in meeting the energy problems of our Atlantic region and of the country as a whole. We must not only be concerned about the supply and the use of our non-renewable energy resources such as oil, gas and coal, but more thought must be given to our renewable energy resources such as tidal and conventional hydro power. As long as the moon is in the sky we will have our tides, and as long as the rains come we will have falling water, all of which can produce energy and can be converted into equivalent barrels of oil, which can be used or sold independently of the whims of the Arabs or any other foreign influence.
The sooner these great sources of renewable wealth can be developed for the benefit of the citizens of Canada, the better. I would suggest that it is time for a policy to be implemented whereby we in this country start to recognize the great and unique potentials which we have in renewable energy resources, and put them to use, rather than letting them go to waste while we use up our nonrenewable resources or import fossil fuels from others at blackmail prices.
As I see our need in the Atlantic region, we should be developing our tremendously large tidal potential as rapidly as possible. Newfoundland in particular has undeveloped hydro potential equal to or greater than Churchill Falls. The extension of very heavy electric transmission grid systems should be part of this program. Our initial surplus of energy should be sold to our neighbours, first to neighbouring provinces and then to the United States on a recallable basis. The price for such energy to the United States should be based upon its alternate cost of generation. We would then be amortizing our capital investment at an accelerated rate during the period of supply surplus to our requirements, and we would be building our plants at lower costs than would be indicated in the future because of our ever persistent inflationary trends.
326

October 10, 1974
The Address-Hon. D. J. MacDonald
The profits which would be accumulated from sale of surplus energy could be used to develop still more of our renewable energy resources.
Through this kind of policy, which would require massive capital expenditure and could only be undertaken by the federal government financing the projects for the provinces, some of the advantages would be: (1), we could make ourselves independent regarding our energy requirements; (2), we could improve our balance of payments position through selling energy which would be initially surplus to our requirements into a receptive market area; (3), we would have for our own use more economic energy, with less risk from ever increasing fuel costs, over a long period of time; (4), we would accelerate the write-off of our investment and have a valuable asset to pass on to future generations; (5), energy would be produced not only on a renewable basis, but also without degradation to the environment; (6), problem of regional disparity of the Atlantic region would be solved. In fact, by development of these resources the Atlantic region could be contributing to the well being of the rest of the country.
A very strong national power transmission system, with inter-connection and ties into a North American continental transmission grid, is greatly needed. Surplus energy from one region would be put into the grid, and areas with deficiencies would buy from the gird. With gas and oil pipelines, which would extend across Canada from coast to coast and allow the flexible interchange of fuels, plus a super electrical transmission grid, this country would lead the world in social and economic development, and our bargaining power, especially with the United States would be greatly improved.
To make use of the advantages which our country has, second to none in the world, we must have more courage in taking our place as world leaders. We must better co-ordinate and stimulate the efforts of industry, government, labour and universities, so that not only may the vast energy potentials of the tides of the Bay of Fundy be developed for the benefit of Canada, but so that we might become less complacent and more innovative.
There must be more research and development in many new technological fields, especially in those fields where we have such tremendous wealth of resources, particularly in the renewable resource areas. Many others will wish to exploit our great potentials. We must be ahead of the pack in technology, in courage, and in management skills in order to protect our environment, to assure that we are not exploited, to assure we assume the kind of leadership that will have great benefit for Canada, and to assure that we use our advantages to give world leadership.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join other hon. members in congratulating our newly elected Speaker, yourself and your associates. I should also like to extend good wishes to our Governor General for his speedy recovery.
I feel I would be remiss if I did not thank the people of Cardigan once again for the honour they bestowed on me, by electing me for the second time to be their representative in Ottawa. The carrying out of my responsibility to

the people of Cardigan is indeed a continuing challenge which I look forward to meeting with renewed vigour in this new Parliament.
Hon. members will recall that a comprehensive development plan for Prince Edward Island was signed in March 1969. During Phase I of the plan many of the programs which have been successful on the Island-are being considered nationally. Phase II, which is now being negotiated, will, I am certain, produce many more programs which can be used by all Canadians. Co-operation between the federal and provincial governements has helped make this plan a success, and the basic plan is being used as a model for agreements with other provinces.
Testimony to the fact that the plan is working is that the number of people leaving the Island has declined substantially, to the point where we now have a real population growth on the Island. This means that a whole new generation of young people can find interesting and challenging opportunities on Prince Edward Island instead of having to move to other parts of Canada or to the United States.
Being from a small geographic area which has an abundance of peaceful charm, we realized that those from large urban areas envy us. We wish to try to avoid some of the mistakes made in those areas by balancing our development and continuing to offer our younger generation better opportunities for work. I want to assure you that we are not prepared to have development simply for the sake of development. What we are looking for are certain kinds of development which will allow us a reasonable standard of living and, at the same time, let us retain and further develop those environmental qualities which have become so precious today.
The basis of Prince Edward Island's economy has long been and will continue to be the agricultural and fishing industries. I am sure that all Islanders applaud the stated objective in the throne speech to increase food production by providing incentives to our farmers and fishermen, including the stabilization of incomes and markets. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has demonstrated great leadership in this direction already.
Island fishermen are extremely pleased with the government's action to ensure Canada's right to manage its coastal resources and environment. Meetings will be held shortly to discuss further measures to conserve our declining fish stocks, as well as the need to regulate licensing of the existing fishery.
Fishermen on the Island are in agreement with the continuing program of up-grading small craft harbours. Results of the last two years are quite evident following federal government expenditures of approximately $1 million on these facilities.
In the government's fight against unemployment, approximately $4 million has been allocated to Prince Edward Island in the Local Initiative Program's budgets of the last three years. Many hundreds of jobs were created during the winters, and the program has been most beneficial to the economy of the area. In the same vein, the Opportunities for Youth program with a budget of $1,300,000 in Prince Edward Island over the last four years, has
October 10, 1974

funded more than 300 projects and made a major contribution toward student employment.
All hon. members must heartily approve the government's projected plans in the housing field to assist those hardest hit by inflation. In line with this, already in this calendar year senior citizens on the Island have learned of CMHC loans to the PEI Housing Authority totalling $2,500,000 for construction of senior citizens' complexes across the Island. The construction of four two-storey apartment buildings in Charlottetown containing 96 one-bedroom apartments, as well as of 38 row housing units in six communities, has been approved for this very extensive program.
This assistance to senior citizens was only one of the measures carried out and planned. Government plans, in this session, regarding increases in maximum pensionable earnings and payments of allowances to spouses of old age security recipients will be very welcome indeed to our elderly.
I also welcome this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to speak to hon. members about the Department of Veterans Affairs.
The senior members of the House are aware that my portfolio includes four other very important agencies which are autonomous but which report to parliament through me. If you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, I would like to describe briefly the agencies and their functions for the benefit of new hon. members who are sitting in this House for the first time. These four agencies are the Canadian Pension Commission, the War Veterans Allowance Board, the Pension Review Board and the Bureau of Pensions Advocates.
The Canadian Pension Commission operates under the legislation contained in the Pension Act. It is concerned with the adjudication of applications for pension entitlement and with the administration of pensions which are granted. I am referring to disability pensions which are awarded as a direct result of injuries, or illness incurred during wartime service. It also awards and administers the pensions paid to the eligible widows and children of those who were killed or died as a result of their war service.
The War Veterans Allowance Board's activities are concerned with the administration of the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. These acts contain the legislation which permits the payment of allowances to qualified veterans and their spouses, or widows and children, who are suffering from economic distress.
They are not to be confused with disability pensions although we do have some cases of veterans who are receiving disability pensions from the Canadian Pension Commission and are also recipients of the War Veterans Allowances.
The Bureau of Pensions Advocates is a publicly financed body whose members prepare and present the cases of veterans, or their dependants who wish to make application to the Pension Commission. It also handles the
The Address-Hon. D. J. MacDonald appeals of applicants who are dissatisfied with the decision of the Pension Commission's entitlement boards.
These appeals are adjudicated by the other autonomous agency in the Veterans Affairs portfolio, the Pension Review Board. It hears appeals against the Pension Commission's decisions, both for entitlement and amounts awarded. It also hands down rulings on matters of interpretation of the pension legislation.
These then, Mr. Speaker, are the other members of the Veterans Affairs family, and I would like to thank the senior members of the House for their patience in listening to the explanation of something that was already familiar to them.
The responsibility imposed upon my ministry by the legislation which has been enacted by previous parliaments of behalf of our veterans and their dependants continues to grow both in complexity and amount. It is not a reducing responsibility, as some might believe, and this fact is borne out by the results of the 1971 census which were released earlier this year.
The 1971 census indicated that there are still nearly a million veterans living in Canada. More than 80 per cent of these are married and many of them still have dependent children. Accordingly, we estimate that there are probably nearly 2 million Canadian citizens who are potentially entitled to one or more benefits under the various pieces of veterans legislation.
To get back to actual figures, there were more than 30,000 veterans and dependants who were active clients of the Department of Veterans Affairs as of March 31 last. These included disability pensioners, war veterans allowance recipients, patients in our hospitals across the country, widows, orphans, children receiving educational assistance and those holding contracts under the Veterans Land Act.
It is not my intention today to describe in detail the many programs and achievements which have had an impact on our veteran population since I became Minister of Veterans Affairs in 1972. I am confident that the record speaks for itself, and I am very proud of that record.
However, I do not want to leave you with the impression that we are a static organization. We are continually trying to improve the legislation covering our veterans and their families to keep pace with the changing social and economic conditions.
I think evidence of this good faith was displayed just last Wednesday when I tabled a bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance and Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. The increases in rates and ceilings, and the other additional benefits included in this bill, were planned many months ago.
I had hoped that this very special group of veterans would be receiving these benefits by now. Unfortunately, the timetable was delayed, as honourable members are well aware. However, I certainly hope that the passage of this bill can be accelerated now so that the thousands of men and women who served our country so honourably and well can soon be enjoying a more rewarding standard of living.

I will continue to consider other legislation and regulations which affect our veterans and their families with a view to making fair and reasonable changes whenever necessary. I would like to tell honourable members that the National Council of Veterans Associations and the Royal Canadian Legion are always most helpful both to me and my senior officials whenever we sit down to discuss matters such as benefits and hospital care for veterans. They are reasonable in their requests and sincere in their motives. They have the interests and welfare of our million veterans at heart, and they have made many significant contributions to what I firmly believe is the best veterans legislation program that exists anywhere in the world.
One of the pieces of legislation in our veterans charter which has been frequently discussed in the past year or so is the Veterans Land Act. I think all members are aware that, last spring, the deadline for those holding qualification certificates to exercise their rights under VLA was extended to March 31, 1975.
The Veterans Land Act was established as a rehabilitation project for those returning to peacetime activities after the end of World War II. It was one of several options available to the discharged servicemen, and it proved very successful for many thousands of our veterans in establishing themselves as farmers or commercial fishermen, or on small holdings. That is what it was designed for and it worked.
Today there are some who are urging that its provisions be extended and increased so as to provide assistance for purchasing retirement homes. It has concerned me that a certain number of people who are advocating these changes in VLA are claiming that my reluctance to change this legislation now is a denial of veterans' rights.
I reject those suggestions completely, Mr. Speaker. The record of this government in the field of veterans legislation has been outstanding. The actions of this administration towards our veterans reminds me of the motto of that famous western regiment, the Fort Garry Horse. It is "non facta verba"-deeds, not words. The government is giving careful consideration to the whole matter of the Veterans Land Act, and an announcement on this subject will be made at a very early date.
There is another aspect to the operation of my portfolio which I would like to mention today. This is our responsibility to those who fell in the defence of our country, and it is our duty to remember and revere their sacrifice.
On November 7 next, with the co-operation of my colleague, the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner), there will be an exhibition of photography on display at the Canadian War Museum. This series of coloured photos will show war cemeteries in more than 70 countries of the world where Canadians, who fought and died in the two World Wars and Korea, are buried. It also has pictures of the principal memorials commemorating those who have no known graves.
At the same time we will be introducing a magnificently illustrated edition of a new publication entitled "Silent Witnesses". This book also honours the 116,000 Canadians who died for the freedom you and I know today but which 
some accept so casually. We must never forget that it was their sacrifice that made it possible.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the privilege of speaking today. I trust I have demonstrated to hon. members that my department is well aware of the obligations it has to those who so gallantly offered their services to our country in time of war. We will continue to honour those obligations.

Mr. Speaker, may I begin by congratulating the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) and his assistants on their appointments. It is with high expectations that I look forward to working with him and the other members of this House. I wish His Excellency the Governor General a speedy recovery.
I also wish to pay tribute to individuals who have had an effect on my seeking public office, individuals such as the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) and the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the former members for the Pembina riding, Mr. Jack Bigg and Mr. Dan Hollands.
I thank the electorate of Pembina. I am conscious of the trust placed in me by them. I pledge co-operation in the House, co-operation between all members of all parties, and although my first concern is the constituency of Pembina, my interests will include all Canadians.
We have had the honour of having both the hon. Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in our constituency. I am sure they will agree when I say that the Pembina constituency is a cross section of people and environments. In it we have a highly industrialized area, a large agricultural area, and densely populated urban areas.
This constituency is a good place in which to live. In some areas it lacks in natural wealth, but an area in which it does not lack wealth is the area of enduring common sense. In these people lie a deep rooted human feeling to do what is best for Canada. They have some old fashioned notions of good manners, honour, and duty towards God and their country. We can learn from them, those of us who run around with our vulnerable egos; we who are more interested in power than in governing.
The purpose of politics is not to justify our own existence but to do something for our country. Our problems will not be solved by legal manoeuvers-they will be solved on the basis of trust. We have a moral responsibility to get our fpodstuff to the people who need it, at a reasonable price. We have a moral responsibility to see that our producer receives a fair return on his product.
Canada is failing in her role as a major world food supplier, and as a leader in the agricultural field generally, because of a lack of leadership from this administration. I suppose the greatest issues in agricultural marketing are the so-called cheap food policies, the evolution of consumerism and the apparent fear that politicians have of the consumer. Events of the past well illustrate this fear; the Nixonomics that affect the beef industry, the U.S. export embargoes, and Canada's export permit system.
It will probably take many more months before order is restored in the marketplace following the chaos that
October 10, 1974

resulted from these decisions. However, I feel that something has happened through all of this that may never be restored at any future date. That something is the faith of the farmer in the systems; his faith in the marketplace and its cycles.
As market forecasters are only too well aware, it is becoming increasingly difficult to predict prices. This fact presents a very large problem to the farmer. We are caught in a real quandary; that of quickly rising production costs and the obvious efforts of governments to protect the consumer from these natural cost increases. These efforts distort normal price cycles as illustrated by the federal government's latest scheme with respect to the beef industry. I fail to see how any politician can be naive enough to think he can increase the producer's returns and still keep down the price at the retail level with a program such as this.
Right now stabilization is, I understand, a big deal in government circles. Of course we all know that it is designed to level out the income of the farmer, but I am not so sure that that means any profitability. From what I can gather from people working in this area, there are a few problems. If production controls are not to be implemented then the profit margin must be minimal in order to prevent overproduction. I must admit that I find the fear of overproduction humourous, because every time one turns around lately it appears as if the government has come back from some great trade mission with news of great market potentials. So what is the worry?
I have not met a thinking farmer yet who really wanted anybody stabilizing his income. Most farmers are entirely competent to look after this themselves. Also, as pointed out previously, when the risk is removed so is profitability, and in this day and age, considering risk, volume of money involved, etc., why should a farmer work for nothing? One of the few drawing cards to farming is potential profit, and to remove that at this time would only guarantee an even greater movement of young people out of farming.
What is rapidly becoming necessary, however, is some form of protection from man made catastrophes in the marketplace, which result in certain segments of the industry losing great amounts of money. An example of what I mean is the U.S. price freeze on beef and its subsequent effects on the beef industry. The interim feed grain policy would also fit into this category, although only in its method of establishing price and not so much the price of grain itself.
I am sure we will see more of these predicaments as food prices continue to rise and governments continue to react. The consumers and governments are only kidding themselves because farm price increases are necessary to keep abreast of cost increases and inflation and, more important, to attract young people into farming.
In 1970 grain was a glut on the market and pig prices were going down. Pigs, however, appeared to be the most practical enterprise in our circumstances. Converting grain to animal products seemed like a logical thing to do because more people wanted pork than barley. Even the government agreed.
The Address-Mr. Elzinga
Everything worked great until last year when the world ran out of grain. As you know, grain prices soared, beef and pig prices dropped, and the grain industry quickly forgot the market it had sacrificed so much to establish. I certainly do not begrudge the grain producer his present prices; they are long overdue, but by the same token he should not forget either that the steer or the pig was his only market not too long ago and could easily be again in the not too distant future.
Contracts that bind the buyer and seller into a pricing arrangement will probably become increasingly important to the producer, especially the young producer, who must protect himself from loss situations. A fine example of this sort of contract that I am a bit familiar with is the hog export program. There is reasonable profit built in, as well as the guarantee of supply, which the buyer is coming to realize as being almost as important as prices.
I hope that if domestic price rises above the export price by a large amount the government will not place an embargo on the export of hogs in an attempt to lower the domestic price. I raise this point because I feel it is a real fear, given the past track record of the federal government. In the Throne Speech the Prime Minister pledged to keep food costs down at almost any cost, and I am sure the farmers' wellbeing will be the first sacrifice in any attempt to achieve this goal.
One observation I have made is that at any given time some segment of the industry is suffering; that is, if the grain producer is making money, the livestock producer is not, or vice versa. There was a brief exception to this recently and during that short period all segments were doing well. The harmony between farmers was great and each appreciated the effort of the other.
If one dare draw analogies, I would like to compare the agricultural industry with the automotive industry. Each separate industry-tire, spark plug, glass manufacturer and so on, supplying something towards the final product, the car-prospers. Why, in food production, must one segment generally be suffering financially?
Personally, I feel agriculture is our most important industry. It is renewable and there is no substitute for food. I feel that the real issue in marketing from now on will be to keep all segments prospering, and I think this should be the challenge.
Occasionally consumers will complain that food costs are too high, but they do not realize that in the cost of a loaf of bread the cost of the cellophane wrapping has risen from 9 per cent of the total cost to 39 per cent. Half of what we purchase at supermarkets is not food but soaps, deodorants, tissues, magazines and other non-food products. It is my hope and belief that Canada, as a whole, will gain substantial social and economic benefits with the revitalization of rural Canada. I hope that those of us here in political office will do justice to this office by thinking beyond today and by stating our fundamental choices for tomorrow.
It is my hope also that we, the politicians, particularly those in leadership positions, will have the courage to spell out the real challenges facing Canada at home and abroad. Inflation is a serious problem, especially for the poor

October 10, 1974
The Address-Mr. MacFarlane
among us. No government can command inflation to go away, but what it can do is give us the leadership required to control it, and that has not been forthcoming from this administration. The growth-rate of Canada's economy is zero, and inflation is over 10 per cent.
Today it is almost a crime for an individual to be a success. It is not right to be thrifty and astute. There are those who would relieve the successful of their life's rewards to give to those who, often through their own irresponsibility, have not reached the same level. Of course, the ones who should be helped are those who have remained at the bottom of the scale through no fault of their own. There is nothing that will squelch human initiative more than a guarantee that the government will look after you. Just remember, all the promises made by politicians will be paid for with public money and not theirs.
It is saddening to think that Canadians take handouts and guarantees of government aid as something honourable. I can remember the day when it was considered something of a shame by those who were proud of their ability to make it on their own. As I have said before, any government which taxes away the rewards of responsible behaviour and effort so that it can remove the penalties for irresponsible behaviour is not something we need or want in Canada.

If you really want to know what the morality of the next generation is going to be, ask them, and you will be surprised. They will tell you. It is going to be a damned fine generation.
They really take their ships and send them across the seas of life; they choose the winds of passion for their sails, and they choose the rudder of reason to steer with. If there is no passion, it becomes an academic, dying argument, so there has to be that mixture. I always used to think when I was at Mount Allison University in the maritimes, when we went out to the lily pond and saw everything quiet and soft on a windless day, "God rests in reason". Then, the wind would come to Sackville, with thunder and lightening, and we would say "God moves in passion". That is what these young people are like. A wonderful mixture. Their sails are set to the winds of passion and their rudders are governed by reason.
The future of this country will be theirs and I should like to think we should run in front of them. It is our responsibility, as my mother and father did for me, to

improve the generation. We should shout over our shoulder of the bright prospect of the future, and of the dangers on the way, so that they may know what our generation has experienced, so that they may have the benefit of our improvement as well as bringing along their own thoughts and ideas.

A young man came to him and said, "Old man, why are you building a bridge? You will never come this way again." The old man replied, "That is so. I am building the bridge for you." This they expect of us. This they demand of us, and this we have failed to do many times. We have a responsibility to leave them something, as my mother left me her music, as my father left me his mathematics, as my minister left me my church. These are important things which will not be dismissed or wiped away.

I believe that sport might just be the replacement for war and conflict in the world. I am one who believes that maybe we shall go to international trade fairs, maybe to international drama festivals and international sporting events-and it will be political, and it should be-but it will be one step for mankind in the direction of ultimately removing the resort to the resolution of conflict by killing one another.
So, sport is important. I am one of those who would like to see it given the status of a separate ministry. I believe it is important enough, for the young people who take part and the old people who watch, that it should stand on its own. I often ask: when Handel wrote The Messiah, did he write about the omnipotence of God, or did God's omnipotence show itself through The Messiah? When Van Gogh painted those olive trees, was he expressing nature or did nature express itself through him? When I coach a football team and I give them a formation, do they express themselves through the formation and therefore find a vehicle for their own expression? I feel that way about athletics, and I think it should be expressed strongly.

subtopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS-SUGGESTED REFORM OF PROCEDURES-GUIDELINES ON ACCESS TO INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC DISCUSSION.
HOUSE OF COMMONS-SUGGESTED REFORM OF PROCEDURES-GUIDELINES ON ACCESS TO INFORMATION-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC DISCUSSION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some might suggest we are moving from the sublime to the commonplace, after that sparkling display of oratory on the part of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane), but there is a relationship between the excellent words of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat and what I have to say, because my topic, too, relates to the institution of parliament itself.
I want to be fairly specific because I have a very short period of time this evening to discuss three items which I very much hope will be before the total House and the committee on procedure when we consider in what ways we can make this institution more vital and responsible in the exercise of its duties.
Sometimes when we talk about traditions and history I think we spend too little time reflecting on the long sweep of change that has occurred in this country and that affects this institution. Hon. members will recall that in the early years of the Canadian nation the budget of this country was something like $20 million. The budget of the country today is something over $20 billion, an increase of some 1,000 times. It indicates to me that the very ability for parliament to be responsible in the exercise and expenditure of public money must of its very nature be exceedingly difficult.
This traditional responsibility of parliament to exercise the power of the purse is one of the basic responsibilities of parliament which I think is not only severely jeopardized but has almost vanished.
Within my time as a member of this place we have abolished the committee of supply, I believe in the year 1969. The committee of supply was abolished for a number of reasons-because it took a lot of time, because the debates related to estimates and expenditures often proved to be rambling, if not meaningless. I believe it was abolished even more so because there were times when the discussion of estimates in the committee of supply was not only embarrassing to the government, but occasionally could prove most difficult when supply was in fact not passed, and the government was on the verge of having to face a very difficult crisis situation where it did not have the money made available by parliament to pay its bills.
What we have in its place over the last five years are 25 allotted days and six votes. This means quite simply that under present conditions the government of the day can ride out the storm on whatever particular issue is brought before it on these allotted days. An indication of how much we have lost, in the sense of controlling the power of

the purse, is the almost total disinterest of the press in those debates. We now have these 25 allotted days and we end up on some occasion, as we will later this month, with a kind of spending orgy that goes on for two or three hours; a whole rash of meaningless votes are taken, and we have the final passage of estimates.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is not being responsible with respect to the way in which we give an account of the expenditure of public moneys. If the power of the purse is vital to an effective working of a realistic parliament, then we will have to look very seriously at how we are going to deal with estimates in the future. I do not have any instant answers, but I do think that this is one of the questions that the committee and all members will have to face.
The second question is access to information. In the last parliament the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), who was then House leader, put before us the consolidation of what has become government practice with respect to the production of papers and the presenting of information. Quite frankly, I think the frustration that has developed in recent years, not only with the oral question period but with written questions and production of papers, relates to the fact that there is this growing amount of information through reports, studies and reviews of one kind and another which the government feels compelled to hide under a great umbrella of confidentiality. We did have, and we have had, a rash of leaks from time to time. Sometimes the leaks are correct; at other times they are incorrect. Again this is an indication of the fact that we have somehow reversed something that is essential to a free and democratic society.
The onus should be on the government of the day-and I do not care which government it is-to prove that a document must be kept confidential because there is some threat or jeopardy to the security of the state itself. I think we have to establish some means whereby that will become established practice, whether it be some kind of independent tribunal which, in effect, will review a decision of government not to put before the public items which it believes are confidential.
The third matter that I raised in my previous question to the Prime Minister and House leader was whether or not in our study of the reform of parliamentary procedures we could not involve a good deal of informed public opinion. There is an awful danger-and I believe all members, if they reflect on this for a moment, will agree-that when you become a member of this institution for longer than a few days-and some of us have been here a good while longer than a few days-it is very easy to rationalize and justify all the intricate and complex workings of this institution.
Of course I know there are many traditions that are worthy of keeping, and some worthy of extending, but we who are in this institution should not feel it is our institution only, or primarily. It is fundamentally an institution of the Canadian people. If they find it confusing, if they find it misdirected and wasting on occasion large amounts of time, if they want to see it sustained and perhaps, from some points of view, resuscitated and restored to an essential area of vitality, then we must have their views.
October 10, 1974

Quite frankly I think if we get early exposure through the media of radio and television this will allow for a good deal more intelligent and interesting comment. I believe that unless we allow others, beyond the members of this place, to comment on reform of parliament itself we will do a great disservice to this institution primarily, and a great disservice to the Canadian people. This is, after all, the House of the common people and a House for the people of this country, and I would urge the government to move very speedily in respect of ultimate reforms for this institution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a very brief reply to the three points that have been raised by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald). The first is that in his description of supply proceedings he only provided about half the description of what actually takes place.
For example, while it is true that opposition parties do have 25 days in the House, there are at least three months in which these estimates are referred to standing committees, committees which have extensive powers to call witnesses, ministers and other people before them to discuss the items in the estimates that committee members wish to have discussed. Whether these opportunities are used is a responsibility that members of the House of Commons must take upon themselves.
One of the reasons for the extension of time, and for moving the work of the committee of supply back into committees, was to provide more opportunity and more time for the House of Commons to cope with the growing volume of legislation that governments have been putting before it.
One of the problems that we face is that the House of Commons is again in danger of being constricted. If one looks at the throne speech one will have to say that in the last two years of minority government, we have discussed in the House of Commons and passed only what was necessary for all of us to get some form of collective record about us. We all must share the responsibility. In the last year and a half of the parliament elected in 1968 the legislative process again slowed down, so we are dealing in the throne speech now with leftovers, tidbits, from the three previous parliaments.
Secondly, I want to comment on the guidelines the government produced last year. They were referred to a joint committee of the House and the Senate. To my knowledge they were never discussed by that committee. I felt that was unfortunate and unnecessary, and I have a commitment from the House leader that at an early date the guidelines will again be referred to the committee. Hopefully that committee will be sufficiently well organized to carry out a discussion, and make a report to the House and to the Senate on the situation.
The last point I want to make is about the meetings of the procedure committee. I quite agree with the point that the public should be invited to participate. I think it unfortunate that during the last two or three years that committee has held so many of its meetings on procedure in camera, a very undesirable practice that I hope will be eliminated in this parliament.

CONSUMER AFFAIRS-SUGAR-CONSULTATION WITH QUEBEC GOVERNMENT TO SETTLE DISPUTE AT SAINT-HILAIRE REFINERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question this morning about the loss of the sugar-beet crop in the province of Quebec did not seem to alarm the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) since he replied that such a loss for the province did not represent 1 per cent of the Canadian sugar consumption.
Mr. Speaker, sugar is one of the main food commodities. Here are some statistics I have in that respect: In 1971 Canada has consumed 1,200,000 tons of sugar, a little more in 1972 and still more in 1973. Thus, the Saint-Hilaire crop represents 2 per cent instead of less than 1 per cent mentioned by the minister this morning.
While Canada is the second largest importer of sugar in the world, the minister finds it normal to learn about the total loss of the sugar-beet crop in the Saint-Hilaire area.
How can Canada ever export sugar if the government does not want to protect that new-born industry which could, in less than ten years, start exporting sugar instead of importing 92 per cent of its consumption?
How can we ever produce our own consumption when it is estimated that Canadian annual needs for sugar will reach 2,500,000 tons within the next 20 years, if we cannot even save a crop that represent only 2 per cent of the Canadian consumption?
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government has left this industry to the hands of pirates here in Canada, who are members of the international sugar cartel, the seat of which is located in England and which is headed by Tate & Lyle Ltd.
Mr. Speaker, I have here an issue dated July 23, 1972 of the London Sunday Times, one of the most important small newspapers in Europe. It carries the following article under the heading, and I quote:
It is interesting to note that this important disclosure of the activities of an illegal cartel involving twenty-two major European sugar companies with an annual market of 600 million Pounds Sterling per annum, should have been totally ignored by every Canadian newspaper,-which resulted in keeping the Canadian public in ignorance of the fact that Tate & Lyle Ltd. was named as a leading participant in the conspiracy, through control of 'SAY' one of France's largest sugar conglomerates.
The Common Market Anti-Trust officials have pointed out, that:-
1.	The refiners pay out large sums of money every year to ensure that there is a unified market.
2.	That 'the refiners maintain high prices and illegal division of market, contrary to public interest'.
3.	That 'this is a Text Book Case of how a cartel and a lobby operate'.
4.	That 'the activities of the sugar refiners involved are the most serious restriction of competition (they) have yet met in the price fixing field'.

Mr. Speaker, these discoveries were made by an English committee commissioned on behalf of the Common Market to make an inquiry into the international sugar

trust; the conclusions of this inquiry were published in the
London Sunday Times.
In a brief presented to the right hon. Prime Minister on February 27, 1973 by the Austin Sugar Refineries Limited of Montreal, which wanted to compete with other companies and offer the Canadian people better prices for sugar, we can read this;

It is a curious fact that in the face of all the representations made by the Consumers Association of Canada, the Industrial Sugar Users Association of Canada, and other public and private groups to Government,-that despite the issuance of the indepth report issued by the Tariff Board Report on Sugar, November 1971, nothing has been done to date by the Combines Department to remove this restriction of trade by Court Action or recommendations to Government concerning the introduction of a National Sugar Policy for Canada.

And, Mr. Speaker, this same company made recommendations, in their brief presented to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Among other things, it is interesting to see what the committee of the House already recommended, which is in publication No. 146 of November 1971, on page 6:

The 362 page report on sugar by the Tarriff Board of Canada recommended the introduction of competition in the sugar industry, stating in part, that-
(a)	The price of refined sugar in Canada does not appear to be related to domestic forces of supply and demand;
(b)	That the domestic price is related to the London daily price for "Free Market Sugar";
(c)	That this situation has the further characteristic that one company is the price leader and the others follow;
(d)	Because of a lack of competition, the Canadian industry has been able to increase its capacity without raising production;
(e)	The structure and behavior of the industry allow the preservation of existing market shares without substantial risk and without the beneficial spur of competitive factors usually prevailing in ordinary markets.

Well, Mr. Speaker, we could continue on and on this discussion to establish that there certainly exists an international sugar monopoly which completely controls from England the South African and Rhodesian sugar markets and which has been granted by our country's special tariff concessions.
Canada could be a sugar exporting country. We have surpluses of maple syrup. Our soil is clearly favourable to the easy growing of sugar-beet. Moreover, we have surplus apples every year. Mr. Speaker, the price of sugar was 1 cent a pound a few years ago and its price has now reached $50 a hundredweight. Yet, the government is doing nothing, as it is under the thumb of international companies and monopolies.
