Mr. Speaker, I must apologize to my colleague if my notes tonight are written in English only. I

am afraid I do not speak French as well as my colleague speaks English, and I congratulate him for this.

The hon. member has wandered somewhat far afield from his original question today about the situation as it existed at St. Hilaire, the refinery in Quebec. In response to the hon. member let me point out first of all that the federal government deplores the existence of the conflict in that place in Quebec, but I think I should reiterate what the minister said this morning, namely, that this is a refinery that is owned and operated by the Quebec government. The conflict at St. Hilaire is a labour problem over which the province of Quebec has complete jurisdiction, and I might say that provinces, appropriately enough, jealously guard their jurisdiction under the BNA Act.
The hon. member states that he is concerned about the effect of this conflict on the Canadian consumer, and that is appropriate enough. I think, however, that it should be put into perspective and noted that there is no shortage of sugar for Canadian consumers. The conflict at the refinery does not affect the price of sugar to Canadian consumers, nor the volume of sugar consumed in Canada, which would otherwise involve the federal government on a Canada-wide economic scale. However, the government appreciates that there does exist a problem for the farmers of the region who are trying to sell their produce.
The hon. member referred to the sugar beet industry. Being myself from southwestern Ontario I can assure him that I have sympathy for those producers knowing the plight faced by them. It is to be hoped that the Quebec government will be able to resolve this dispute at an early date.

subtopic: FINANCE-ALLEGED DENIAL OF LOANS BY CHARTERED BANKS UNDER SMALL BUSINESS AND FARM IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS
FINANCE-ALLEGED DENIAL OF LOANS BY CHARTERED BANKS UNDER SMALL BUSINESS AND FARM IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in the adjournment debate, and I want to say how pleased I am to see my colleague, the honourable member from southwestern Ontario, in his place to respond. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) on his appointment as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, and to tell him that I wish him well.
On October 8 I directed a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) with respect to certain chartered banks in this country denying loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This is a very unfortunate situation and it is one that warrants immediate and effective attention from the Minister of Finance and the government. I well recall the concern with respect to this matter expressed by many of my colleagues on this side of the House in the Official Opposition during the debate on Bill C-14 last spring. The main thrust or purpose of Bill C-14 was to raise the ceiling on the amount of 8!4 per cent money that chartered banks can loan to these two important, but seldom recognized, segments of our economy. When one observes the past statistics, one continues to wonder, however, just how useful these programs really are.
October 10, 1974

Referring to the 1972 bank report, we note that under the Small Businesses Loans Act less than 2,900 loans were granted in all of Canada. One major chartered bank granted a sparse 134 loans.
It is not unusual or difficult for many honourable members to cite examples from constituents which clearly indicate that banks are less than interested in these two government programs, and indeed a similar scheme, the Fisheries Improvement Act, could be included as receiving this same type of cold shoulder reception.
Chartered banks often react in general terms with responses like, "We've never heard of the program before", or "It's not our policy to loan money under these programs" or "Our allotment of funds for such purposes has been fully allocated".
With attitudes and responses like these, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Minister of Finance that these programs cannot be fully utilized, so the amendments in Bill C-14 become actually useless.
I suggest that, because of this situation, the Minister of Finance should make either strong and effective representation to the banks to correct this matter, or provisions ought to be introduced and incorporated into Bill C-14 to assure that banks and lending institutions be required to make available sums of money to their clients under these programs.
Another real problem is the lack of information regarding the number of applications and inquiries made to banks, and the number refused. I would be willing to expect and admit that some were rejected for good reason, but this information should be available if we are to develop fully the kinds of programs and policies that best meet the needs and financial requirements of these industries.
Let us remember, Mr. Speaker, that these segments of our society form the backbone of our economy. They provide strength and stability to our Canadian commerce. They create over half of our Gross National Product and employ over half of the working people of Canada. They are entitled to better treatment than they have received and are receiving.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-ALLEGED DENIAL OF LOANS BY CHARTERED BANKS UNDER SMALL BUSINESS AND FARM IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my thanks to the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) for his kind comments on my appointment as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. I should also like to compliment him for bringing this matter up in the House, and not being satisfied the answer, again bringing it up on what has been called "the late show." I think the matter warrants airing and public scrutiny.
Adjournment Debate
The Farm Improvement Loans Act and Small Businesses Loans Act have been in effect for many years, and I am sure that members are reasonably familiar with them. They will recall that last spring the acts were amended following a full review by the government in order to expand their scope and increase their effectiveness and usefulness to borrowers.
These acts have played a useful role in meeting the credit requirements of a large number of Canadians. The Farm Improvement Loans Act has been particularly important as a source of intermediate credit to farmers. Up to the end of June this year, loans extended under FILA totalled over $3 billion, so I think that contradicts what my hon. friend has said. In fact it has been found useful. Such loans reached a record of $230 million in 1973.
Since inception of the Small Businesses Loans program over $300 million was lent to June, 1974. This is another indicator that it is being used. Lending under this program has been rising sharply in recent years, and was over $30 million in 1973.
In the first six months of this year lending under these programs declined. I think that is what my hon. friend is endeavouring to highlight. This may well have been due to a reluctance by lenders to participate in the programs because of a growing differential between the rates they were permitted to charge at that time and commercial rates of interest. In this respect, hon. members may be aware that the permissible rates are determined twice a year, on April 1 and October 1, on the basis of a formula contained in regulations. The formula rate is the average yield on government of Canada bonds during the six months preceding the rate change, plus 1 per cent.
It will be noted that, due to the averaging period, the formula rate will lag behind current commercial rates when the latter are changing rapidly. This lag became significant in the first part of 1974 when the bank prime rate moved from 91/2 per cent in January to 11 'h per cent in July. During this period the rate for the vast majority of these guaranteed loans, all except those for the purchase of land under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, was 8 'A per cent until March, and dropped to 8 per cent on April 1. Thus the formula rate became increasingly out of line with rates charged by lenders on regular loans, and by July the negative differential had become quite significant.
